articles.title: In Moldova, teens are learning about democracy and elections through an app
articles.author: Daria Dergacheva
paras: The app gives short, interactive lessons using quizzes, flashcards, and other easily accessible formats in three languages
Originally published on Global Voices
Screenshot of views of VotEDU on the App Store. Fair use.

This interview is part of a series of spotlights on the work of some of the grantees of the Digital Spark granting scheme, as part of the Regional Support Mechanism EECA project, implemented by the Metamorphosis Foundation and TechSoup, in partnership with CIVICUS and under the Digital Democracy Initiative (DDI) that covers the Global South. It is being published on Global Voices as part of a content-sharing agreement.

Moldova is a relatively small post-Soviet state with a population of three million people. A landlocked country, it has a long border with war-torn Ukraine and Romania; with the latter, it shares the same official language. The territory that is now Moldova was once part of the Russian Empire, and later the Soviet Union, and Russia has been meddling in its affairs.

Moldova has a large Russian-speaking population and a problematic unrecognized territory: Transnistria, which is basically controlled by Russia. It also has European aspirations and was officially named a candidate to join the European Union in 2022, after Russia invaded neighbouring Ukraine.

The country’s most recent parliamentary elections were held in September 2025, and despite the record influx of Russian disinformation and other meddling, elections were recognized as fair and democratic by the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OCSE) observers. The pro-European Party of Action and Solidarity (PAS) won the elections with a small majority.

The initiative supported by Digital Spark is an app called VotEDU, which answers basic questions about the democratic institution of elections for high school students in Moldova. It does so through short, interactive lessons using quizzes, flashcards, and other easily accessible formats in three languages: Romanian, Russian, and English, and is the subject of this Spotlight story.
Global Voices interviewed the app’s developer, Vlad Garbuz, about the impact of Digital Spark and his initiative.
Global Voices (GV): Please tell us about your organization and why you chose to get involved with the Digital Spark project.

Vlad Garbuz (VG): I started VotEDU, an independent civic-education project in Moldova, to help young people understand democracy before they vote for the first time. The idea began at the VOTech hackathon in Moldova. I joined Digital Spark because I wanted to turn it into a tool that students could use in everyday life and teachers could bring into class. The project helped me build the app and begin testing it with the young people it is meant for.
GV: What issue or challenge in your community prompted you to undertake this project?

VG: Young people meet politics every day through their feeds, long before they enter a polling station. In Moldova, many young people encounter misleading claims online. Yet many have very few easy ways of asking questions about elections and getting the answers they can understand. That made me wonder how civic education could reach young people in the spaces where they already spend their time. VotEDU was the answer. It puts short lessons, simple explanations, and activities on their phones, so they can learn at their own pace.
GV: What are the key changes or activities that you implemented during your participation in the project?

VG: During Digital Spark, VotEDU developed into a civic-education app with nine units, 28 short lessons, quizzes, interactive activities, and a glossary of 136 civic terms. The content is available in Romanian, Russian, and English. All of the lessons have been reviewed for accuracy and political neutrality. Student privacy guided the app’s design. A short guide was also prepared for teachers. VotEDU was represented at Moldova Digital Summit 2026, where several educators expressed interest in trying it in schools. The app is now being piloted with high school students in Moldova through its web version. It is also available on the App Store, with the Google Play version coming soon.
GV: How did your participation in the project impact your beneficiaries and the community you serve? Please provide examples.

VG: Teacher feedback has highlighted the need for digital tools alongside Moldova’s electoral education textbook. VotEDU brings these topics into a format students can explore on their phones. High school students in the pilot program are using the app and sharing feedback. The feedback tells us how easy the information was to access, as well as appreciation of the app’s design, quizzes, and illustrations. Together with teachers’ suggestions, this feedback is helping improve the content in the app and making it a better user experience.
GV: How has your own knowledge, awareness, and experience with digital democracy and civic space changed?

VG: I have learned that the design of a civic tool is part of its message. If an app is hard to understand, available in only one language, or careless with privacy, it may leave out the very people it hopes to reach. Building VotEDU has made me more careful about how I explain civic topics. Each lesson needs to be accurate and fair, while still being simple enough to use on a phone. I now think more about whether young people feel comfortable asking questions and forming their own views, not just whether the information is online.
GV: What are the most valuable lessons and experiences you are taking away from this project?

VG: The lesson I will carry forward is to start earlier. Young people should have a chance to understand democracy before an election campaign is asking for their attention. I have also learned that a good idea needs to be tested with the people it is meant to help. Building VotEDU was only one part of the work. Now students are using it and telling us what they think. Their experience will help us see what works, what is still unclear to students, and what needs to change.
GV: What comes next? How will you apply the learning and digital capacity you have built?

VG: I will continue the pilot program and use feedback from students and teachers to improve VotEDU. I plan to bring it to more schools, including rural schools, and use short questions before and after the lessons to see what students learn. In October 2026, I also demonstrated VotEDU at MEGAPHONE & e-Society in Skopje. I showed how digital tools can make civic education more useful and engaging for young people, and inspire others to try similar ideas. VotEDU is a project that can be adapted for different countries and topics. Making the project public and accessible is one of my objectives to ensure anyone can easily build something that will bring benefits to their local community.

articles.title: Fossil fuel lobbyists are trying to derail climate action once again at COP31. Can they be stopped?
articles.author: Christian Downie, Professor of Political Science, School of Regulation and Global Governance, Australian National University
paras: This week, it was revealed that 100 corporations and industry groups tied to fossil fuel interests – including the US multinational ExxonMobil and French energy company TotalEnergies – have sent delegations to this year’s global climate summit COP31 in Turkey.

These climate talks have a long history of lobbyist interference. More than 1,600 fossil fuel lobbyists attended the COP30 talks in Brazil last year, and more than 1,700 at the 2024 talks in Azerbaijan.

This is a problem. The whole point of these long-running United Nations negotiations is to address human-caused climate change, which is primarily driven by burning oil, gas and coal – the very products these lobbyists are paid to promote.
At COP31, fossil lobbyists will have been hard at work promoting fossil fuels. Their methods often draw on what academics call “discourses of delay”.

This is how it works. To slow the shift away from fossil fuels, lobbyists spread disinformation, such as claiming fossil fuels are part of the solution (“gas is a transition fuel”), that future technologies will save us (carbon capture), or we’re doomed and it’s too late to act. Oil and gas companies have dramatically increased their Google ads in the month leading up to COP31, for example.

Researchers have shown fossil fuel lobbyists use a two-pronged strategy. First, they point to a lack of international action as a reason for not acting on climate change at home. Second, they work to stymie progress at the same international talks.
A new UN report says it’s now too late to hold the global temperature rise to 1.5°C. The world will likely pass this threshold in 2030.
A big reason for this is obstruction by lobbyists of climate policies that target the root cause of climate change – fossil fuels.
So, why are fossil fuel lobbyists allowed into these talks?
At last year’s COP30 summit, host country Brazil tried to push back against fossil fuel lobbyists.
Alongside the UN and UNESCO, Brazil launched an international partnership to counter climate change disinformation and misinformation.
Thirty countries have since signed onto the declaration, which calls out the:

growing impact of disinformation, misinformation, denialism […] and other tactics used to undermine the integrity of information on climate change, which diminish public understanding, delay urgent action, and threaten the global climate response and societal stability.
Lobbyists gain access to the talks in different ways, including through affiliations with non-governmental organisations and industry groups and as part of official government delegations.

While this year’s draft negotiating text makes reference to information integrity, there’s still no clear code of conduct or meaningful disclosure of fossil fuel industry ties for the thousands of delegates attending COP31. There are no clear, explicit rules against spreading climate disinformation.
A long history of lobbying

Sadly, this story is all too familiar. For as long as there have been international climate talks, fossil fuel lobbyists have tried to persuade countries not to act with the urgency the science demands.

It took more than a quarter of a century of climate talks before fossil fuels were explicitly addressed at the Glasgow COP in 2021. Until then, the focus was on greenhouse gas emissions – but not the fossil fuels causing them.
Corporate fossil fuel lobbyists have been assisted by so-called petrostates, such as Russia and Saudi Arabia, whose economies are highly dependent on oil and gas production.
And when the oil- and gas-producing states Azerbaijan and the United Arab Emirates hosted the COP talks in 2023 and 2024, respectively, both countries used the summit to push new fossil fuel deals.
What are lobbyists targeting this time?
There are more than 100 different agenda items up for debate at COP31, many of which are opposed by fossil fuel lobbyists.
Negotiators are still discussing a UN initiative designed to rapidly increase efforts to cut greenhouse gas emissions, for instance.

Alongside the official agenda, COP President and Turkish Environment Minister Murat Kurum released a separate “action” agenda organised around ten themes. Some of these, such as transitioning to clean energy, threaten fossil fuel interests.

Fossil fuel lobbyists will likely try to block calls for phasing out coal, gas and oil – just as they did last year, where Brazil’s efforts to formalise a roadmap transitioning away from fossil fuels ran aground.
Another concern for fossil fuel interests is the electrification goal, aimed at boosting electricity’s global share of final energy demand to 35% by 2035.

If this translates to more electric vehicles, batteries and heat pumps in homes and electric furnaces in factories, it would mean less demand for oil and gas. That would affect profits for companies such as ExxonMobil and Shell.
Australia on the tightrope
Australian Climate Change Minister Chris Bowen is acting as president of negotiations at COP31 as part of a co-hosting arrangement with Turkey (also known as Turkiye).
This represents a tightrope walk for Australia.

Domestically, the Albanese Labor government is attempting to speed up the energy transition. Policies such as subsidising home batteries have proven a strong success. More than 600,000 households have installed batteries since the program began last year. Electric vehicle uptake is rapidly accelerating.

Internationally, however, Australia remains one of the world’s largest coal and gas exporters. State and federal governments keep approving new projects. Given this, many countries have questioned Australia’s climate credibility, especially its Pacific neighbours.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese was heavily criticised for failing to mention fossil fuels in his opening COP31 speech. Just minutes before Albanese spoke, UN Secretary-General António Guterres urged countries to make fossil fuels “go the way of the dinosaurs”.
“The dinosaurs did not have a lobby. Fossil fuels do,” he said.
Can progress be made despite lobbyists?
As COP31 enters its final days, the eyes of the world will be on Australia and Turkey.
Should the co-hosts fail to get agreement on concrete steps to advance Brazil’s latest efforts to transition away from fossil fuels, many countries will be left disappointed.
But despite the best efforts of the fossil fuel industry, momentum for a shift away from oil, gas and coal is gathering pace outside the UN talks.
In April, nations attended the first international conference on transitioning away from fossil fuels, while the Fossil Fuel Non-Proliferation Treaty Initiative continues to gain members.
As always, though, much more needs to be done, and quickly. Clamping down on lobbyists and climate misinformation is well overdue.
Christian Downie receives funding from the Australian Research Council.

articles.title: An AI chatbot can explain your rights. But can it get you justice?
articles.author: The Hague Institute for Innovation of Law (HiiL)
paras: Getting information does not equate to accessing justice
Originally published on Global Voices
Image courtesy the Hague Institute for Innovation in Law

This post is part of Global Voices’ November 2026 Spotlight series, “Justice as infrastructure.” In this Spotlight, Global Voices is partnering with The Hague Institute for Innovation of Law (HiiL) to highlight the ways justice functions as critical infrastructure for any society. You can support this coverage by donating here.

Imagine a woman facing eviction who turns to an AI chatbot for help. It explains her rights and drafts a letter to her landlord. But she cannot afford a lawyer, does not know where to submit the letter and has no institution that can enforce her rights fairly. The chatbot has made the law easier to understand, but has it brought her any closer to justice?

A September 2026 study by UK organization JUSTICE and the Administrative Fairness Lab found that one in six UK respondents who had experienced a legal dispute had used an AI chatbot. Researchers examined 77 conversations involving questions about rights, legal correspondence, complaints and court proceedings. Yet they could not establish whether these interactions helped resolve the disputes. We know more about how people use AI for legal help than whether it changes their circumstances.

That distinction matters. An estimated 1.5 billion people worldwide cannot obtain justice for their problems. HiiL’s Justice Needs Surveys, covering more than 150,000 people across 20 countries, show that only around four in 10 achieve a fair resolution. AI could help address this gap, but it is important to understand where its contribution begins and ends.
The promise of AI for justice seekers

People facing legal problems may not know whether what happened to them is unlawful, where to seek help or how to navigate an unfamiliar process. Legal advice is expensive, services can be difficult to reach, and institutions intimidating.

Purpose-built AI tools can explain rights clearly, organize information, prepare documents and identify relevant services. Voice-based tools may also reach people with limited literacy or without smartphones or reliable internet.

Early pilots are yielding promising results. In Australia, Hear Me Out, developed by the National Justice Project and the University of New South Wales, helps people identify the appropriate complaints body, understand the process and prepare supporting documents. Its pilot assisted more than 400 complaints, helping people turn experiences of injustice into complaints that can be pursued. In Nigeria, Citizens’ Gavel’s Podus AI helps people understand their legal rights, draft petitions and complaints, and identify the government agencies responsible for addressing them. Since its launch in March 2024, the platform has onboarded more than 33,000 users.
These are meaningful developments. But the number of tools and people assisted tells us only part of the story. What happens after someone submits a complaint?
When an answer is not a resolution

Understanding rights does not mean being able to exercise them. A tenant may know an eviction is unlawful but have nowhere to turn; a small business owner may prepare a claim but lack the means to pursue it. A person experiencing domestic abuse may face practical, financial or safety barriers to seeking protection.

Another challenge is getting the other party to participate. In dispute resolution, this is known as the “submission problem,” a concept developed by economists William Landes and Richard Posner. A process works only if both parties are willing to negotiate, accept mediation, or submit to a third-party decision. AI may help prepare a claim, but it cannot persuade a landlord to negotiate, compel an employer to pay wages, or make a business respond. Even when parties reach an agreement, there is no guarantee it will be respected. Without mechanisms to support compliance and enforce outcomes, an agreement on paper may have little practical effect.

There is also a growing challenge for the institutions receiving complaints. AI may make it much easier for people to submit them, potentially increasing demand on already overstretched public services. Recent UK reporting describes public bodies, councils and courts receiving a growing volume of AI-assisted submissions, some lengthy, repetitive and difficult to assess. Dubbed “AI clog,” the issue is not that more people are complaining — lowering barriers to redress is positive. The problem is that institutions may lack the capacity and resources to respond.

If AI increases the number of people approaching public authorities, those authorities must be equipped to meet the demand. This requires more than using AI to summarize documents or automate responses. It means better-designed complaints processes, adequately resourced institutions, trained staff and clear pathways for handling cases. Otherwise, technology risks making it easier to submit a complaint without making public services any more responsive.

Sustainability is another concern. A HiiL policy brief highlights the dependence of AI tools on external providers, proprietary platforms and uncertain funding. If a provider withdraws a service, what happens to the people relying on it?

HiiL’s exploration of voice-based AI support for local justice actors in Niger illustrates this risk. The aim was to make legal information available in local languages and support community intermediaries. But technology embedded in proprietary infrastructure can be difficult to maintain or transfer when a provider withdraws.

Ownership and governance therefore cannot be afterthoughts. Local justice providers and institutions need control over their tools, legal knowledge and data, as well as the resources to maintain and adapt services. Otherwise, technology intended to improve justice delivery may create new dependencies and disappear when people need it.
Making AI work for people seeking justice

AI for justice should be measured by more than chatbots launched, queries answered or documents generated. We need evidence that tools help people prevent problems, reach appropriate services, secure the participation of other parties and achieve fair outcomes.

This requires investment in tools designed around people’s problems and the providers best placed to address them. AI should connect users to human assistance, complement formal and informal justice mechanisms, and be supported by safeguards, accountability and sustainable financing. Crucially, public institutions must also be equipped to handle the increased demand that easier complaints procedures may generate. Evaluation should ask whether AI improves outcomes, for whom, under what conditions and at what cost. AI can make legal help more accessible and help people take action. But its promise will depend on whether the wider justice system can respond.

The ambition should not be to give everyone a free AI lawyer while leaving them waiting for an answer from the institutions responsible for upholding their rights. It should be to use technology to help those institutions work better, address people’s needs and deliver on their responsibilities fairly and effectively.

articles.title: ‘Who will respond?’: Jailed Hong Kong pro-democracy activist Joshua Wong fears being forgotten amid 10-year sentence
articles.author: Hong Kong Free Press
paras: The activist admits his mental state has been negatively affected by the 10-year sentence increase
Originally published on Global Voices
Joshua Wong released from Lai Chi Kok Reception Centre on June 17, 2019. HKFP's File photo.

This article was originally published by Hong Kong Free Press on November 16, 2026. The following version is edited and republished on Global Voices under a content partnership agreement. It is also part of Global Voices’ November 2026 Spotlight series, “Justice as infrastructure.” You can support this coverage by donating here.

In a letter from a Hong Kong prison earlier this year, jailed activist Joshua Wong expressed dread over the looming sentence in his foreign collusion case. “Fretting about whether it’s 2032 or 2037, my mental state is hardly all right,” he wrote in Chinese, weighing when he might regain his freedom.
The agony inevitably stems from this: What if it’s 2037? Well, it’s easy [for people] to sympathise in the moment, but it’s difficult to be consistent, and it will only get harder.

The 30-year-old pro-democracy activist has already spent almost six years behind bars over various offences and was set for release in January 2026, until authorities charged him last year with conspiring to collude with foreign forces — the second case against him under the Beijing-imposed national security law. His case is one of the most high-profile examples of changing judicial norms in Hong Kong.
A prison letter Joshua Wong wrote to friend and former fellow student activist Louis Lee in February 2026. This photo was taken on September 30, 2026. Photo by Kyle Lam/HKFP. Used with permission.

On November 5, just two months before he was due to be released, a court sentenced him to 10 more years in prison for colluding with foreign forces. He is now expected to serve until late 2036, when he turns 40.

Standing in the courtroom as his new sentence was announced, Wong shook his head slightly and made notes, but appeared calm. Judge William Tam ruled that Wong’s offence was one of a “grave nature” under the national security law, which carries a minimum penalty of 10 years in jail and up to life imprisonment.
The judge knocked off three years from a 13-year starting sentence for Wong’s guilty plea.

In prison correspondence shared with HKFP by two close friends ahead of Wong’s sentencing, the former poster child of Hong Kong’s democracy movement had at times reflected on the weight of facing an additional decade behind bars. He expressed anxiety over fading from the memory of his friends — and from society at large. In one letter, Wong wrote:
I have no idea how much more I will lose in the passing of time. Responsibility is, in fact, response-ability. But who will respond? I can’t help but ponder and doubt.

Once a pro-democracy activist dedicated first and foremost to Hong Kong’s political future, Wong began campaigning as a charismatic, eloquent student leader who dared to stand up to the authorities — even to Beijing. Hong Kong is an overseas territory of China, and has increasingly been pressured to conform to China’s political goals in recent years, despite agreements that Hong Kong would retain “a high degree of autonomy” when handed over to China in 1997. A Netflix documentary about him is succinctly titled “Joshua: Teenager vs. Superpower.”

Yet, after years behind bars, Wong has changed. The teenager who focused single-mindedly on Hong Kong’s democracy movement has become even more caring for those around him despite being separated by prison walls, according to his friends.
Tiffany Chin, a former student activist who campaigned alongside Wong, said. The pair were once romantically involved and are now friends. She shared:
For me, it doesn’t feel like we’re the only ones supporting him. In fact, he has been supporting people on the outside in his own way.
And, with the political causes he once championed now firmly crushed, Wong has turned inward to reflect on himself. In another letter, he wrote:
We had held such high aspirations for society from a young age, we should hold ourselves to the same standard. Only by refusing a life of mediocrity can we be worthy of the world we envisioned.
From “robot” to caring friend

On a bright summer day in June 2025, while serving a sentence for subversion at Stanley Prison, Wong was arrested behind bars and brought to court the same day on a fresh charge of conspiracy to collude with foreign forces.
The prosecution came without warning. That day, Chin and Louis Lee, another longtime friend of Wong’s, rushed to the court after hearing the news, but failed to see him in person.

Authorities accused him of conspiring with Nathan Law — another high-profile, pro-democracy student activist — in 2020 to collude with foreign elements, citing Wong’s sharing of Law’s social media posts calling for international sanctions against Hong Kong as evidence.
The unexpected new charge was devastating to Wong. That month, he confessed he was under a lot of pressure — a vulnerability he rarely showed in the past, Chin said.

After so many prison terms and all the ups and downs over the last decade… he seldom openly showed vulnerability. So when he felt the need to say so bluntly that he was not OK, I truly believed he wasn’t.

Having begun campaigning at the age of 14, Wong has been in and out of prison throughout his years of activism. He now has a total of eight criminal convictions, including three separate offences linked to unlawful assembly and two national security offences.
Joshua Wong is photographed inside the Lai Chi Kwok Reception Centre on March 4, 2021. Photo via HKFP. Used with permission.

Born in 1996 to a Christian family – one year before Hong Kong was handed over to China from British rule – Wong rose to prominence in 2011 when he co-founded student protest group Scholarism amid a public outcry against a proposed patriotic education curriculum.

The following year, Scholarism activists occupied the forecourt outside Hong Kong government headquarters and staged a hunger strike to protest what they described as a “brainwashing” curriculum. In a widely reported encounter, the teenager Wong twice refused to shake hands with then-city leader Leung Chun-ying, who visited the protest site alongside education officials.
Hundreds of thousands of people rallied behind Wong and his fellow student activists, forcing the government to back down and shelve the proposal.

But the teenage campaigner was also viewed as somewhat distant and domineering among the inner circle of Scholarism. Lee, who mainly handled protest logistics at that time, described his relationship with Wong as “almost like that of a boss and subordinate.”

Chin, who joined Scholarism around 2013, similarly described Wong as a deeply rational figure who seldom expressed his emotions. “Ten years ago, everyone described him as someone without many feelings,” she said. “Like a robot.”
Wong might even come across as “rude,” she added, noting that he rarely said thanks to others during that period.

A large part of Wong’s youth coincided with a period of escalating social movements in Hong Kong. Just two years after the anti-patriotic education protests, the city saw the 79-day Umbrella Movement in 2014. Wong, then aged 17, took centre stage in mobilising public support for student protesters, who demanded democratic reform and universal suffrage.

In a demonstration that sparked the Umbrella Movement, Wong and other student leaders led protesters into the forecourt of the government headquarters in an action dubbed “Reclaiming Civic Square,” seeking to escalate their campaign. That eventually resulted in Wong’s first criminal conviction.

In 2016, Wong and fellow student leaders Alex Chow and Nathan Law were found guilty of unlawful assembly. Though initially spared prison, Wong later served around 69 days behind bars – his first jail term – following a government appeal in 2017. His penalty was ultimately quashed by the Court of Final Appeal in 2018.

Scholarism disbanded in 2016. Wong and several former members, as well as young activists like Law, went on to establish Demosisto, a political party advocating for “democratic self-determination” in the city. Wong served as general secretary.
Lee and Chin did not join the new party, and they grew estranged from Wong during that period.

That year, Law was elected to the Legislative Council, making him the youngest lawmaker in Hong Kong history at the age of 23. He won over 50,000 votes, giving Demosisto a strong popular mandate. The prospect of youth democracy activism appeared bright at the time, but Law was eventually disqualified from his seat in 2017 following an oath-taking controversy.
From left: Joshua Wong, Agnes Chow, and Nathan Law, photographed on March 10, 2018. Photo via HKFP. Used with permission.
It was only after Wong’s detention in late 2020 that Lee and Chin reconnected with him, beginning with an exchange of letters.

In 2019, citywide protests and unrest triggered by a controversial extradition bill engulfed the city. Wong and Demosisto were heavily involved in the protests, with the activist frequently lobbying foreign governments to impose sanctions on Hong Kong officials and halt the export of crowd control equipment to the city’s police force.

Then, in June 2020, Beijing imposed the national security law, effectively crushing political dissent in the city. Demosisto disbanded on the eve of the law’s enactment, while Nathan Law left Hong Kong in self-exile.
For Chin, the catalyst for reconnecting with Wong was realising how much their relationship meant to her following his incarceration.
We were like family to each other. And I felt it was time to resolve our past grievances and carry on our relationship. Not a romantic one, but one with the kind of care you find in a family.
Tiffany Chin uploaded this photo of herself and Joshua Wong after Wong was sentenced to 10 years in jail for foreign collusion. Photo via HKFP. Used with permission.

Their correspondence, Chin said, focused mostly on daily life – the routine details of what was happening on both sides of the prison walls. Some of those Chin received stretched across multiple pages, covered in Wong’s slightly angular handwriting.
A major change in Wong, Chin noticed, was how often he reflected on his past interactions with people, rather than his public advocacy.

He has changed quite a bit after nearly six years in prison. Like I said, he would reflect on things he didn’t handle well in the past. Age is certainly a factor. But, like he said, he has had plenty of time to contemplate now. One of the big differences is that he has cherished his connections and bonds with friends even more.
Meanwhile, Lee’s exchanges with Wong centred on their wide-ranging shared interests, touching on everything from Taiwanese politics and Japanese idols to popular anime series and Cantopop.
While in prison, Wong was charged with conspiring to subvert state power under the national security law, in a landmark case known as the “Hong Kong 47” – a reference to the number of defendants.

The defendants were prosecuted over an unofficial primary in 2020 aimed at fielding viable candidates, in a bid to secure an unprecedented legislative majority for the pro-democracy camp. Once achieved, the camp had planned to veto government budgets and force the chief executive to resign.
Wong was among those who pleaded guilty before the trial opened. In 2024, he was sentenced to four years and eight months in jail.
Lee and Chin both described Wong as being “prepared” for the subversion term. Chin said:

He was able to predict a range within which the sentence would fall. And eventually his prediction was just two months off. You weren’t overly worried about him. Because at that time you had the feeling that he was capable of handling this, both physically and mentally.
Wong even started imagining what he would do after his release in January 2027, Lee said, before the new charge dimmed his hope.

In September, Wong pleaded guilty to the collusion offence. His lawyer argued for a sentence of less than 10 years, submitting that his role in the conspiracy was limited and that the activist demonstrated genuine remorse.
At times, he has lamented the dwindling attention he receives over the years. Chin said:

He once mentioned that, for him, not receiving letters meant not feeling cared for. Some people might have written at first, but gradually stopped… He certainly never feels people have a responsibility or obligation to write to him, but the reality is that fewer have.
The uncertainty of a potentially heavy sentence has weighed on Wong and his close friends. Lee noted that many mutual friends had either left the city or drifted away:
Honestly speaking, not only does he worry about a long jail term, those of us on the outside also worry that one day we may no longer be able to help as we enter new stages of life.
It was a “great pain” to face the years ahead, Chin said. Lee said he would wait for Wong’s release for as long as it takes.
Louis Lee, photographed on November 12, 2026. Photo by Kyle Lam/HKFP. Used with permission.

articles.title: Diversifying funding was supposed to protect civil society: It did not
articles.author: Forus
paras: ‘…stability, where it exists, is only ever twelve months deep’
Originally published on Global Voices

Activists hold a candlelight vigil to commemorate those who lost their lives in post-election violence in Tanzania in Nairobi, Kenya, on November 20, 2025. Image by Anadolu Lucas-Mukasa courtesy of FORUS.
By Clarisse Sih, Bibbi Abruzzini, and Jake Wieczorek
“Every one of our grants is annual and project-tied. We have no reserves and no core funding, which means that stability, where it exists, is only ever twelve months deep.”

That is how one civil society organization in Algeria described its finances to us in a recent survey. It is a sentence many donors would recognize from their own grant files, and it captures a reality familiar to many organizations: years of navigating short-term grants, restricted budgets and uncertain renewals, with little room to plan beyond the next funding cycle.

For years, civil society organizations have been encouraged to diversify their income, develop new partnerships and build financial and capacity resilience. But the latest — and many would argue the chronic — funding crisis is exposing the systemic retreat in development funding. Alternative sources are scarce, civic space is under pressure, and the political environment is becoming increasingly hostile.
A shock on top of a squeeze

Official development assistance fell by more than 23 percent in 2025, the largest annual drop ever recorded, and is projected to fall even more in 2026. Twenty-six of the 34 members of the OECD’s Development Assistance Committee cut their aid, and the US aid freeze that flooded headlines turned out to be just one part of a wider retreat.

To understand what this means in practice, the European Union System for an Enabling Environment for civil society (EU SEE) consortium partners — Hivos, Forus, Democracy Reporting International, European Partnership for Democracy, Transparency International and Civicus surveyed organizations in their networks between August and September, receiving 195 responses from over 68 countries.

The findings reveal the scale of the disruption: three-quarters of respondents say their funding is lower than at any point in the past decade. A third say more than half of their budget has been affected since January 2025, and 86 percent report harder terms, such as grants not being renewed, being reduced or cancelled or even more complicated compliance terms.

“The results show a perfect storm for civil society. Funding is disappearing at the very moment many organizations are facing greater political pressure. What’s being lost is not just programs and jobs, but the independent voices to defend rights, give voice to vulnerable communities, and hold power to account,” explains David Kode, program director of EU SEE.

The hardest hit were mid-sized, locally rooted organizations, despite having the most diversified funding. Among them, 90 percent reported funding cuts, 77 percent lost staff or reduced programs, two-thirds scaled back advocacy and community outreach, and 59 percent became less vocal publicly.
These are organizations connecting communities with services, donors and local governments.

Responses to question 11 in the survey: From January 2025 until today, what percentage of YOUR organization's budget has been impacted by donor budget cuts? Budget impact differs across organizational profiles. Screenshot from the survey. Fair use.
“We have had to sacrifice even our own salaries from other private sources to keep the NGO open and those who received a monthly salary are now working ad honorem,” said a respondent from Honduras.
In Indonesia, some organizations put staff on unpaid leave, while others could pay only half of their employees’ salaries.

Yet the damage is not only monetary: almost half of respondents report reduced capacity for advocacy and about 40 percent say they have become less vocal or reduced their reach. A third of the respondents report having less control over their own priorities, and some have moved away from contested areas of work to keep their funding.

At the same time, almost two-thirds say civil society work has become less safe since early 2025, with more than half reporting more scrutiny, harassment or legal and administrative restrictions and half pointing to narratives portraying civil society as foreign-influenced.

This reflects a wider deterioration in the environment in which civil society operates. As one respondent from Zimbabwe put it: “The current funding crisis should not be viewed only as a financial challenge; it is fundamentally a civic space and democratic governance challenge.”

“An enabling environment is not simply the existence of a supportive policy. It is being able to register without unnecessary obstacles, access resources without compromising independence, speak and organise safely and meaningfully, influence decisions that affect communities — and knowing that when risks emerge, there are institutions and partners willing and able to respond,” says Marie L’Hostis, program and advocacy director at Forus.

These narratives do not stay rhetorical for long. The relationship between funding and civic space is particularly visible where governments are introducing or enforcing restrictions on organizations receiving resources from abroad.

In El Salvador, President Nayib Bukele accused journalists and civil society organizations of misusing USAID funds as part of a global money laundering operation, just as the US aid freeze hit. A few months later, the Legislative Assembly approved a Foreign Agents Law requiring anyone receiving funds from abroad to register and pay a 30 percent tax on those contributions.

By September 2025, long-standing organizations had begun to close: FESPAD, founded in 1988, and FUDECSO, after 33 years of work, both announced their dissolution, citing legal uncertainty and an unsustainable financial burden.

In Uganda, the proposed Protection of Sovereignty Bill 2026 would require any individual or organisation receiving money from outside the country, even from Ugandans living abroad, to register as a “foreign agent” and seek ministerial approval. In a country where most NGOs depend on foreign funding, that turns the loss of donor money into a question of legal survival. Foreign agents laws are spreading, stigmatizing civil society and choking the funding that remains.

The consequences extend beyond the loss of individual projects. David Kode warned that the current crisis also involves “an erosion of relationships” and a breakdown of trust between donors and civil society.

A separate Forus report, “Strengthening the Enabling Environment for Civil Society: Evidence and Priorities for Action,” reaches a similar conclusion: abrupt funding shocks are not simply financial setbacks but structural threats to civil society’s independence and ability to act.
As report researcher Nicole Walshe put it during the launch, “without the resourcing, there is no civil society.”

The report points out that “these shocks transfer risk to local actors and weaken institutional capacity.” How long funding lasts, how restrictive its conditions are and who decides priorities all shape whether civil society can advocate, organize collectively and hold decision-makers to account.
So, what would make a difference?

Donors should protect continuity before disruption becomes irreversible: bridge funding, early warning of cuts and responsible exits. They should make compliance proportionate to context and risk, and fund legal, physical, and digital protection. The respondents call on national governments to protect access to domestic and foreign funding and the freedom to speak.

Governments can deepen the crisis or soften it. In Botswana, as international donors including USAID withdrew, the government reduced its own funding to civil society, including cutting all funding to the Botswana Council of Non-Governmental Organizations (BOCONGO), the national umbrella body. Organizations that support some of the country’s most vulnerable communities were left with neither international nor domestic support at the very moment both were needed most.

For Chris Nkwatsibwe of Uganda’s National NGO Forum (UNNGOF), civil society needs predictable, multi-institutional financing, alongside reserves that allow organizations to withstand political pressure and financial shocks. Domestic resources and alternative forms of ownership are equally important to reduce dependence on foreign funding and accusations of foreign influence.
“What kind of financing can now enable civil society to really genuinely remain independent, but also continue thriving in conditions of civic restrictions?” Nkwatsibwe asks.
The opportunity is to move from funding civil society to sharing power with it: in decisions, resources and defining success.
As Forus Co-Chair Moses Isooba told the Aid Matters 2026 conference in Vienna, “Power moves when three things change: who decides, who holds the resources and who defines success.”

In Morocco, Latifa Soufiani of Espace Associatif called on international donors and financial institutions to make respect for freedom of association central to their cooperation with governments. “We must be present to make our voices heard,” in international cooperation, she argued.

Luisa Rodríguez Táriba of Venezuela’s Sinergia highlighted how shrinking international support is undermining organizations’ ability to maintain teams and sustain both humanitarian and civic space work. As she observed, “The reduction of civic space doesn't happen overnight. It is multifactorial and happens over time.”

Despite the pressures, she offered a reminder that should remain at the centre of funding decisions: “The most important thing is people” and the communities they are part of must come before institutions, priorities and funding agendas.

articles.title: Beijing has three priorities at the Shenzhen summit – a China expert explains
articles.author: Tom Harper, Lecturer in International Relations, University of East London
paras: China is hosting the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit for the third time in the past 25 years. The gathering in Shenzhen will see the leaders of the US, China and Russia sit down together for a formal three-way meeting for the first time in history.

But what does China want from the summit? I see it as having three main priorities. First is to consolidate its position as one of the world’s most important diplomatic hubs. Second is to set out its vision for a new global order.

And third is to take advantage of favourable geopolitical conditions, primarily brought about by US setbacks in Iran and Russia’s quagmire in Ukraine, to adjust the terms of its engagement with Washington and Moscow.

Hosting national leaders and other high-level officials has become a key feature of Chinese diplomacy in recent years. President Xi Jinping has welcomed over 25 world leaders to China so far in 2026. These include Canada’s Mark Carney, Germany’s Friedrich Merz, Spain’s Pedro Sánchez and the UK’s former prime minister, Keir Starmer.

Beijing’s push to become a key diplomatic convener is a notable break from earlier forms of Chinese diplomacy. In the 2010s, the assertive and confrontational approach of Chinese officials on the international stage was widely known as “wolf warrior” diplomacy.

The name is derived from a series of patriotic Chinese action films, also called Wolf Warrior. In this period, Chinese officials used social media to share controversial political memes and spar with foreign politicians and critical journalists, drawing condemnation in diplomatic circles.

This belligerent approach was retired in the early 2020s. Notable wolf warriors such as China’s former foreign affairs minister Qin Gang and ministry spokesman Zhao Lijian were reassigned or removed from their posts.
China’s hosting of the latest Apec summit is in line with Beijing’s new diplomatic strategy, suggesting it has acknowledged the limitations of the wolf warrior approach.
2. Reshaping the global order

As well as showcasing China’s shifting approach to diplomacy, hosting major international events such as the Apec summit is a central part of Beijing’s wider ambitions to reshape the global order – most notably as a venue to gain greater legitimacy for its vision.

This vision was summarised in a 45-page white paper released by China’s state council in June. The paper signalled the Chinese government’s desire to evolve from being a participant of the existing international system to the architect of a new global order where China and the global south play a greater role.

The same message was repeated in the run-up to the Shenzhen summit. In a speech in late October, China’s foreign affairs minister Wang Yi declared that “the rise of the global south is the most momentous shift since the second world war”.

He framed China’s hosting of multilateral events such as Apec as a vehicle to give developing countries a greater voice on the international stage. It is this vision that China seeks to convey to the wider world through the Shenzhen summit.

The timing of the Shenzhen summit works in China’s favour. With the US and Russia currently bogged down in costly military conflicts in Iran and Ukraine respectively, and Trump reeling from a punishing electoral defeat, it is Xi who holds the strongest geopolitical hand.

When Trump, Putin and Xi sit down together in Shenzhen on November 19, China may be in a position to push harder on the terms of its engagement with Washington and Moscow. A primary goal for China is to stabilise the global economy, which has been disrupted by the war in Iran.

However, many commentators remain sceptical that the three-way meeting will deliver any concrete outcomes. The US and China recently extended their fragile trade truce, delaying the expiry date until January 2027. Preventing relations from deteriorating is thus probably in the interests of both countries.

And on various other issues, the three leaders are entering the meeting with vastly different ambitions. Trump is focused primarily on agreeing a three-way nuclear arms control agreement. But China has historically refused to discuss any limitations on its nuclear arsenal while its stockpile of warheads remains smaller than the US and Russia’s.

On the other hand, Russia has pushed to make Ukraine a central part of the talks. It is aiming to build support for a settlement to the war on terms favourable to Moscow. However, China has sought to keep Ukraine off the agenda entirely, fearing political backlash and deeper economic countermeasures from the EU should it back such a settlement.
Regardless of this, the 2026 Apec summit offers a window into what China hopes to achieve on the international stage as well as the world it perceives itself to be in.

Tom Harper does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: Xi-Trump-Putin summit: when great powers want to call all the shots, what does it mean for everyone else?
articles.author: Alexander Korolev, Associate Professor in Politics and International Relations, UNSW
paras: Xi Jinping, Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump are meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China, on Thursday.
The meeting is no doubt unusual – a very rare opportunity for the leaders of the world’s three major powers to exchange views directly on major global issues.

It’s drawn comparisons to the Yalta conference of 1945, when US President Franklin D Roosevelt, British Prime Minister Winston Churchill and Russian leader Joseph Stalin met to divide the world into spheres of influence after the second world war.

But this is no Yalta 2.0. Nor is the Shenzhen summit an isolated episode. In May this year, Xi hosted back-to-back visits by Trump and Putin to Beijing. Trump reciprocated by hosting Xi in Washington in September, and met with Putin in Alaska last year.

Taken together, these developments signal a broader shift away from the post-Cold War emphasis on global institutions and multilateral consultations toward a more personalised form of great power management.
This is likely the new normal: a world in which China, Russia and the US act as an informal steering committee for global affairs, with Europe and other middle powers increasingly on the sidelines.
Who’s invited into the room

While China, Russia and the US remain strategic competitors, they increasingly share an understanding of how international politics should be conducted: less through institutions and coalitions, and more through direct engagement among a small number of major powers.

This is by no means a formal alliance – not even between China and Russia – or a coordinated redesign of the international system. Rather, it reflects a common instinct toward great-power management of international affairs.

All three favour a world in which major powers enjoy special rights and a privileged voice in shaping outcomes, negotiating major questions directly while limiting others’ involvement. Whether discussing war, security issues or economic stability, the major powers increasingly appear willing to bypass institutional channels in favour of high-level, direct diplomacy.

For instance, Russia and the US just concluded a third round of peace talks this year in Abu Dhabi towards ending the Ukraine war. While Ukraine was part of the discussions, European negotiators were not.
In such a world, power determines not only outcomes, but who gets invited into the room when outcomes are being discussed.
Europe increasingly on the sidelines
The most obvious casualty of this trend is Europe.

During the Abu Dhabi talks last week, the Russian delegation made clear it wanted a new security framework for Europe modelled after the spheres of influence that existed during the Cold War. Trump has also flagged this as a possibility, saying the US was working on a big deal to end the war that would include “all of Europe”.

After the talks, US special envoy Jared Kushner said Washington wanted Europe to be part of the process. He added, however, that finding someone who could credibly speak for Europe might be harder than persuading Russia to include them – a provocative statement.
These comments have set off alarm bells in Europe and reinforced a growing perception that Europe is increasingly fragmented and marginalised as an actor in global politics.

More significant, however, is that Xi ultimately agreed to join the Shenzhen trilateral summit. Having seen Europe sidelined from the Abu Dhabi talks, his decision to meet with Trump and Putin risked legitimising that exclusion, even if Ukraine is not on the agenda.

That looks awkward for China, given Xi’s repeated emphasis on multipolarity and criticism of Cold War-style politics dominated by a few major powers. Beijing has also previously stressed that Europe should be “at the table” for Ukraine discussions.

And yet Xi has agreed to meet with Trump and Putin. Moreover, China’s Foreign Ministry described the summit as having “groundbreaking significance”. The three leaders would “exchange views in depth on safeguarding world peace and promoting strategic stability in major-power relations,” it said.
This suggests Beijing accepts a model of diplomacy centred on major powers, to the exclusion of others.
And this creates an uncomfortable reality for Europe.
Europe remains one of the world’s largest economic and technological centres, but it struggles to translate that weight into a unified strategic voice that carries weight on the global stage.
The symbolism of the Shenzhen meeting is telling. Three leaders will be discussing issues that affect Europe’s future. And again, Europe itself will not be present.
The middle powers’ counter-agenda

However, the return of great-power diplomacy does not mean middle powers are irrelevant. European nations, Canada, Australia, Japan, South Korea, and key Southeast Asian nations may not have the military capabilities or geopolitical heft to alter the distribution of power in the international system.
But they do still have institutions, networks and coalitions. They can help shape international rules, sustain institutions and build partnerships capable of constraining larger states.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney’s call for closer middle-power cooperation reflects this logic. Rather than choosing sides in the great-power rivalry, he’s recognised the necessity to “stop pretending, to name the reality” while “building coalitions that work – issue by issue, with partners who share enough common ground to act together.”

The more global power becomes concentrated in the hands of a few leaders, the stronger the incentive for middle powers to work together. They are unlikely to decide the overall direction of the world order, but they can still influence the rules, norms and institutions through which that order operates.

The question raised by Shenzhen, therefore, is not whether a handful of major powers will continue to exercise disproportionate influence. They will. Rather, it is how the rest of the world will respond.

Alexander Korolev receives funding from 2026 Strategic Policy Grants Program (SPGP) grant from the Australian Department of Defence for the project Strategic Hedging Under Pressure: Survival Strategies for Smaller Powers.

articles.title: Street medicine vendors are dangerously filling Haiti’s healthcare gaps
articles.author: Jude Pierre Louis
paras: The ongoing security situation has made the country’s healthcare crisis worse
Originally published on Global Voices
Image by Global Voices, created using Canva elements.

Haiti is a country with very few health facilities and a dearth of healthcare workers to meet people’s needs. Public hospitals lack basic medical equipment, demand far exceeds staff capacity, and administrative problems are rife.

Other health centres, usually run by non-profit organisations, help some of the most vulnerable people, while private hospitals are few and far between, given that most Haitians cannot afford to pay for treatment there. Even the wealthy are often forced to go abroad for treatment when faced with critical health issues.

This already dire situation became worse when gangs from the Viv Ansanm criminal coalition began targeting both public and private health facilities, looting many of them, stealing equipment, and even setting fire to some of the properties. Health centres located in gang-controlled areas are often forced to close temporarily because of fights that break out between rival gangs.

Enter the challenge of street medicine vendors, mobile drugstores, and sellers operating from kiosks. Practically everywhere you go — on sidewalks and public markets, inside bus stations and more — you can find hucksters selling medicine out of buckets and bags, or from small stalls. These vendors have no professional medical training; yet they often “prescribe” drugs that have nothing to do with their customers’ health concerns. Sold in questionable conditions on the street, in heat and dust, these “medicines” pose a serious danger to consumers’ lives.

No Haitian government has fought effectively against this issue. Because most people cannot afford private health centres, they self-medicate, taking these drugs without medical advice. In many cases, the drugs are either expired, spoiled, fake, or do not work as promised. While licensed drug stores are operating, they are small in number compared to the many unauthorised vendors that line the streets.

In a YouTube video on the channel Sedney the Reporter with host Sedney Saint-Fleur, Dr Wellington Derameau, a doctor, pharmacist, and researcher who completed several specialised university training programmes in the United States and France, spoke about the problems in Haiti’s pharmaceutical sector.

That public concern over low-quality medicine led him, in collaboration with the University of Colorado and the Faculty of Medicine at the State University of Haiti, to test the quality of pharmaceuticals circulating across Haiti, particularly in the capital, Port-au-Prince. In 2020, they published the first scientific paper, showing the results of tests in which researchers sampled roughly 258 boxes of antibiotics across 28 open-air markets in Port-au-Prince:

Nou te jwenn 6 antimikwobyen (antibiyotik) sou 11 ki pa t gen okenn konfòmite spèktr. Sa vle di, lòske nou fè des analiz poussées, nou wè ke medikaman sa yo nou te ranmase nan lari a yo pa gen anyen pou wè ak medikaman, pa gen prensip aktif.

We found that six out of 11 antibiotic types failed basic spectral compliance testing. Advanced laboratory analysis revealed that these street-bought products contained no active ingredients whatsoever.

Selling drugs without active compounds in this informal market leaves patients without effective treatment and accelerates antimicrobial resistance. Dr Derameau highlighted cases where patients bought “amoxicillin” expecting a functioning antibiotic, but received capsules filled with starch:
Mache paralèl la fragilize mache legal la, se premye konsta pa m pa rapò ak sa, epi li mete an evidans movèz kalite medikaman yo.
The parallel market undercuts the regulated sector, directly contributing to the spread of substandard medicine.

Official statistics from the Ministry of Public Health and Population (MSPP) for the 2025–2026 fiscal year underline the scope of the problem. Across the nation, only 101 pharmaceutical companies, 49 storage drugstores, 49 import agencies, and three local manufacturing labs hold valid licenses, while some geographic departments lack any legal pharmaceutical representation.
This vacuum, Dr Derameau emphasised, feeds a real threat to public health:
Donc le constat est criant par rapport avec la non-réglementation des pharmacies dans le pays, tout sa pral anjandre nou avèk yon cercle vicieux de vente illicite des médicaments.
The lack of pharmacy regulation creates a glaring threat, trapping the country in a vicious cycle of illicit medicine sales.
Compounded by widespread gang violence and insecurity, these unregulated sales leave the population without reliable access to essential healthcare.

Dr Derameau shared a sad anecdote from his time at Hôpital Universitaire La Paix, involving a child suffering from acute glomerulonephritis. Curious why the patient was not improving, he asked the parents to show him the medicines they were administering. Upon checking, he saw that the medicine was inappropriate for the child’s condition and did not match what had been prescribed. If he hadn’t discovered this in time, it could have led to the child’s death, and nobody would have known the cause because of the absence of forensic facilities in the country:

Mwen pa bezwen di'w ki kantite lòt moun ki viktim, chak desè ta sipoze dokimante pou ale gade koz ki alawouz li malerezman, c'est pas le cas, mwen pran egzanp grenn echantiyon sa donc mwen menm mwen veku, men pa bezwen di'w ki kantite lòt moun ki viktim pa rapò avèk movèz medikaman.

I do not need to tell you how many other people are victims; every death is supposed to be documented to look at the root cause, but unfortunately, that is not the case. I take this single example that I personally experienced, but I do not need to tell you how many other people are victims because of bad medicines.

The child’s parents bought the medicine from a street vendor stationed directly in front of the public hospital, where it is common to find small kiosks and mobile vendors offering different types of medication, and using loudspeakers to advertise all kinds of drugs for various illnesses.

The lion’s share of medication being sold on the Haitian market, Dr Derameau said, comes from India and the Dominican Republic (DR). However, there are also many products with no listed origin at all, which he considers an anomaly. Authorised pharmaceutical laboratories respect quality standards, he explained, as do legitimate importation agencies. The vulnerable area, however, is the border, which serves as the main entry point for contraband.

Although quality control and verification institutions exist alongside the national laboratory as public bodies responsible for regulating the importation, manufacturing, and sale of medicines, this does not stop all kinds of drugs from circulating freely on the market without any real oversight.

Even as he stressed that not all medicines imported from the Dominican Republic are sub-standard, Haiti is flooded with many low-quality drugs, especially when it comes to medications that are in high demand. From his work experience at the Justinien University Hospital in Cap-Haïtien, Dr Derameau also discovered that many of these medicines are not registered with the Ministry of Public Health:
Yo soti nan lòt sirkwit la atravè les fwontyè yo. Gen des laboratwa an Repiblik Dominikèn k ap ponpe nou des medikaman ki pwòp pou Ayiti.
They enter through the other channel across the borders. There are laboratories in the Dominican Republic pumping out medicines made specifically for Haiti.

Noting that generic medicines manufactured by local pharmaceutical laboratories — which number three in total — are very good and respect quality standards, he also posited that there is an industry manufacturing fake medicines within Haiti itself, and called on the state to investigate.

The security crisis is not helping matters. Roads leading to the Great North and Great South — as well as parts of Port-au-Prince — are controlled by various gangs, creating a major obstacle for the free movement of medicine, as well as access to health centres and other distribution points. He highlighted the sabotage and looting that many pharmacies suffered in downtown Port-au-Prince:

Chaîne d'approvisionnement an, insécurité a gen anpil enpak sou li, donk li kraze disponibilité médicaments yo, donc patient vin soufri, marché noir fèt ak médicaments sa yo. Imajine'w tout pharmacie ki te anba lavil la ke bandi yo kase (piye). Gen lòt fenomèn, se machann kap vann nan bus yo kap chanje dat expiration médicaments yo epi y ap vann yo. Donc insécurité a impacté qualité de vie moun yo, insécurité a impacté qualité soins yo, insécurité a impacté protocole thérapeutique yo.

The security crisis heavily impacts the supply chain, thereby destroying medicine availability, causing patients to suffer, and creating a black market for these drugs. Imagine all the pharmacies downtown that bandits looted. There is another phenomenon where vendors selling on buses change the expiration dates on medicines and sell them. So insecurity impacts people’s quality of life, insecurity impacts the quality of care, and insecurity impacts therapeutic protocols.

The challenges around transporting medicines also drive black-market demand and further increase border contraband. Yet Dr Derameau says he is optimistic that if the state shows real political will and enforces strict regulations, it can end these practices.

articles.title: In win against impunity, Indonesian court orders the reform of Military Justice Law
articles.author: Mong Palatino
paras: The court ruled that soldiers who committed criminal offenses should be tried by civilian courts
Originally published on Global Voices
Constitutional Court of Indonesia in Jakarta. Photo by Christophe95. Wikipedia. CC BY-SA 4.0

This post is part of Global Voices’ November 2026 Spotlight series, “Justice as infrastructure.” In this Spotlight, Global Voices is partnering with The Hague Institute for Innovation of Law (HiiL) to highlight the ways justice functions as critical infrastructure for any society. You can support this coverage by donating here.

Indonesia’s Constitutional Court ruled that the 1997 Military Justice Law would be invalid unless amended within two years. The decision was hailed by human rights groups because it means soldiers who commit crimes can be tried in civilian courts.

Article 9 of the Military Justice Law requires active-duty personnel of the Indonesian National Armed Forces to be held accountable exclusively under the military justice system, even when they commit ordinary criminal offenses and human rights violations.
The law was a legacy of the New Order era when the country was under the strongman rule of Suharto, who relied on the military establishment to hold power from 1966 until his resignation in 1998.

The October 15 court ruling was celebrated by human rights groups that have long advocated for the overhaul of the law. They have documented how military courts have failed to investigate and prosecute grave abuses committed by soldiers. They have also expressed concern that military judges are active-duty soldiers, and that judicial investigations and prosecutions often take place within the military chain of command and behind closed doors, with no public oversight.

One of the petitioners asking officials to revoke the law was Eva Meliani Pasaribu, the daughter of Tribrata TV journalist Rico Sempurna Pasaribu, who was killed in June 2024 after reporting about a gambling operation allegedly involving a high-level military official. The military conducted a closed-door investigation and dismissed the allegation for lack of evidence.
Ibnu Syamsu Hidayat, the legal counsel for the petition, addressed the court during the hearing and explained how the law erodes civilian supremacy within a democratic system of governance.

“The dominance of military court jurisdiction over the general judiciary is considered inconsistent with the principles of a constitutional democracy, which mandates that civilian authority must take precedence over military power.”
Hidayat added that the law’s broad provisions have been interpreted to include other criminal offenses committed by soldiers.

“It allows them not only to try military personnel or those equated with them for military crimes and disciplinary violations, but also to adjudicate other criminal cases such as corruption, traffic offenses, domestic violence, narcotics, psychotropics, and child protection cases.”

During the hearing, numerous high-level military officers spoke up in defense of the law. The director general of Defense Forces at the Ministry of Defense, Marshal H. Haris Haryanto, argued that the actions of soldiers, including criminal violations, “can also affect the solidarity and readiness of the military institution.” He added, “Military courts are designed to understand these characteristics so they can deliver decisions that satisfy a sense of justice while also taking into account the interests of national defense.”

The commander of the National Armed Forces, General Agus Subiyanto, said the petition questioning the effectiveness, independence, and accountability of the military justice system “is not based on a comprehensive understanding of the characteristics of military law.”

He emphasized that military judges have the independence of judicial power guaranteed by the constitution and are under the technical judicial supervision of the Supreme Court, adding, “In a military organization, discipline is the primary foundation of national strength. Therefore, the commander’s authority to ensure due process for his subordinates is an inherent legal obligation to maintain operational readiness and the institution’s honor.”

Legal experts who participated in the hearing disagreed, arguing that the law needs reform in order to comply with current human rights standards. Al Araf told the court that the law was drafted under the framework of an “authoritarian political regime” that ignored the principles of rule of law.

“During the New Order era, the legal products enacted in the form of statutes tended to be repressive and merely served as instruments of control for those in power,” he said. “The state enacted laws not within the framework of the rule of law, but solely to fulfill the needs of the rule by law.”
Zainal Arifin Mochtar, another legal expert at the hearing, said the law has to be updated to conform with democratic principles.

“Many issues have emerged, ranging from dual jurisdictions, a lack of synchronization with the spirit of reform, the absence of detailed regulations regarding connectivity, to the issue of independence and accountability of military justice, which is often discussed as a form of legal exceptionalism,” he said.

The move has been widely celebrated by human rights defenders. The Indonesian human rights group KontraS welcomed the court decision, noting that one of its employees has been subjected to an acid attack perpetrated by a group of soldiers. Under the new ruling, soldiers could be tried in public courts in such cases.

“This ruling closes a legal loophole that has long been perceived as protecting individual soldiers from accountable law enforcement, while also marking a new chapter in upholding the rule of law and fulfilling the mandate of security sector reform in Indonesia,” read their statement.
The reform is the result of decades of work and activism, as explained by Human Rights Watch (HRW).

“Justice for civilian victims of military abuses shouldn’t be blocked by an unfair military court system,” read their statement. “Amending the law on military justice will support efforts begun decades ago to ensure the Indonesian military is a professional, credible institution whose soldiers are held accountable when they commit serious abuses.”
Free Press Unlimited said the court ruling is a victory against impunity.

“The Constitutional Court’s eagerly awaited ruling is a true victory for justice and a critical step for Indonesia in its fight against impunity,” read their statement on the ruling. “We urge lawmakers to act promptly and adhere to this landmark ruling as soon as possible. Only then can Indonesia finally turn a corner and ensure that cases involving military personnel will be dealt with by civilian courts, as it should be.”

Both Indonesian and international civil society groups are urging lawmakers to start the reform process by consulting the public and various stakeholders. Activists argue that public vigilance has to be sustained, especially since Indonesia’s current president, Prabowo Subianto, is a former general dismissed from the military for committing human rights violations. Since coming to power in 2024, he has expanded the military’s role in civilian governance.

articles.title: Jensen Huang scandal illustrates why human nature is cybersecurity’s weakest link
articles.author: Vanessa Bohns, Braunstein Family Professor and Chair of Organizational Behavior, Cornell University
paras: The end of Jensen Huang’s tenure at Nvidia is steeped in irony. The chief executive of a company whose growth has been propelled by the seemingly unstoppable rise of artificial intelligence was brought down by a vulnerability that no algorithm can eliminate: human nature.

Huang’s resignation from the chipmaker he co-founded followed reports of multiple affairs, most notably one with Alice Huang, a business executive whom U.S. authorities suspect of spying for China. The company says no secrets were leaked.

In a world increasingly focused on protecting private information against high-tech hacking schemes, Huang’s downfall is a reminder that, as the infamous hacker Kevin Mitnick observed, the “human factor is truly security’s weakest link.”

Huang is hardly the first person in a powerful position to lower their defenses. In 2023, Italian Premier Giorgia Meloni spoke candidly about foreign affairs in a call with Russian pranksters who recorded and released the conversation. In 2011, former CIA Director David Petraeus gave his biographer, with whom he was having an affair, access to notebooks containing classified information.
These cases raise an important question: Why would someone with an entire security apparatus at their disposal let their guard down in an ordinary conversation or an intimate moment?

Part of the answer comes down to the ways in which we are wired to react to other human beings. As a social psychologist who studies how people respond to requests, I’ve seen how a human voice, a simple touch or the mere physical presence of another person can be persuasive. Social cues that increase a sense of familiarity and intimacy can make people feel safer, more trusting – and more willing to hand over money, comply with requests, divulge information or take risks.
The comfort of a human voice

Mitnick has been called “the most notorious hacker of all time.” Until his arrest in 1995, he spent years gaining access to privileged information at companies such as Nokia and Motorola. He pulled off his espionage not by writing sophisticated code-breaking software but by having conversations with his targets.
He would call people up and talk them into handing over their passwords by claiming to be the new IT guy or someone’s boss’s colleague. The people he spoke to overwhelmingly believed him.
In other words, Mitnick recognized the power of the human voice.

Studies show that hearing a person’s voice, as compared to reading their written thoughts, makes that person seem more capable and relatable. Interactions via phone, video chat and voice chat also create stronger social bonds than the same kinds of interactions via text or email.

Perhaps for these reasons, people are more effective at persuading others to do things for them over the phone compared to when they make the same requests by text. In a study I conducted with social psychologist Mahdi Roghanizad, participants asked other people for favors through randomly assigned communication channels. They received about twice as many “yes” responses over the phone as they did by email.
When it comes to obtaining company secrets or circumventing export laws, a human voice may be all you need. And that isn’t the only edge people have.
Studies have found that human touch can also have surprising effects on tipping behavior, acquiescence and risk-taking.

In a famous 1984 study, a server who lightly touched diners as she handed them their change received bigger tips. In another classic psychology study, female experimenters approached 178 strangers and asked them for change to use a nearby pay phone. When the experimenters lightly touched the arm of a person they approached, that person was 76% more likely to agree to give the change.
The researchers theorized that these light touches created a sense of familiarity. That familiarity, in turn, made people more willing to open their wallets.

Other research suggests that light touch can also make people feel safer and more willing to take risks. In a 2010 study, participants were more willing to take financial risks when a female experimenter gave them a light, comforting pat on their shoulder.

Perhaps the most well-known study of influence, Stanley Milgram’s infamous shock experiment, illustrates how much it can matter to be in the room when you ask someone to do something they may be feeling uneasy about.

In the original study, an experimenter stood behind participants and instructed them to administer purportedly dangerous shocks to someone they thought was just another participant. The experimenter asked participants to incrementally increase the intensity of the shocks. Nearly two-thirds of participants went all the way to the highest shock setting. In a variation of the study, however, the experimenter left the room and gave instructions over the phone. In this version, only 22.5% went that far.

Although researchers continue to debate how to interpret Milgram’s findings, my colleagues and I have similarly found that people are far more likely to say yes when we ask them to do something face-to-face.

In one study, participants who made requests in person were 34 times more likely to get a yes than those who made requests by email. In another study, in-person requests were significantly more effective than requests made over the phone or video call.

Cyberattacks and phishing emails pose real threats to security. But sometimes the biggest threats come from the people in the room with you. While we don’t know exactly what transpired between Jensen Huang and Alice Huang, her proximity to the Nvidia CEO illustrates a vulnerability that even the best cybersecurity measures can struggle to guard against.
