articles.title: Fighting in Yemen has made crossing the Bab el-Mandeb even more dangerous – jeopardizing aid and refuge for millions
articles.author: Lauren Carruth, Associate Professor of International Service, American University School of International Service
paras: In recent days, Iran-backed Houthi forces have gained greater control of the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, a vital hub of trade, travel and migration between the Middle East and Africa.

The partial closing of the Strait of Hormuz as part of the war in Iran – and escalating conflicts in Yemen, Ethiopia and Eritrea – had already brought this narrow waterway into new global prominence. Control over the Bab el-Mandeb Strait remains critical to military operations and commodity markets throughout the region.
However, the Bab el-Mandeb’s strategic geopolitical and commercial shipping importance has largely overshadowed its role as a critical humanitarian corridor.

Bab el-Mandeb means “gate of lamentation” or, more poetically, “gate of tears” in Arabic. It remains one of the most dangerous migration passages in the world. Last year, more than 900 people died or went missing trying to cross. In October 2026, a boat capsized off the coast of Djibouti carrying nearly 300 people, many of whom were escaping violence and persecution.
Meanwhile, millions of people in Yemen and throughout the Horn of Africa face destitution or death without access to lifesaving deliveries of humanitarian relief supplies shipped through the strait.

Our years of research and forthcoming book “Refugees Without Refuge” demonstrate how the Bab el-Mandeb Strait is key to the lives of millions of people throughout the region seeking safety, opportunity and humanitarian assistance. Protecting the safe movement of people and goods through the strait is key to averting future tragedies.
A corridor for travel, trade and escape

Located at the southern mouth of the Red Sea, between the arid coastlines of Eritrea, Djibouti and Yemen, the Bab el-Mandeb Strait connects the Indian Ocean to the Red Sea and Suez Canal. On a clear day along the wide beaches and mangrove forests on the coast of Djibouti, you can see the sandy hills on the shores of Yemen, only about 20 to 30 miles away. On starry nights, the scattered lights of coastal towns twinkle across the waters.

For centuries, passage through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait has been vital to global trade in salt, spices, coffee, livestock and other goods. Religious pilgrims, travelers, migrants and traders have long used the strait for relatively easy transport between continents.
Today, people crossing the strait are also escaping poverty, war, political persecution, disasters and gender-based violence.
Hot, tired, financially depleted and frequently sick or injured, refugees and migrants traverse the Bab el-Mandeb at all hours.

Most negotiate passage across the strait on derelict boats with “delalas” – facilitators, brokers or smugglers – in the shadows of coast guard and police patrols and outside United Nations and governmental migration controls.

The numbers of people crossing the strait are difficult to estimate. Between January and August 2026, the U.N.’s International Organization for Migration recorded 122,258 arrivals to Yemen from the Horn of Africa – even more than had crossed by that time in 2025. Most of these migrants were from Ethiopia, and most traveled without passports or visas.

Since August, displacement and insecurity throughout the region has worsened, making accurate figures for the numbers of people migrating and the numbers of people dying trying to cross impossible to estimate.
A lifeline for those escaping conflict

Despite the dangers of this crossing, the Bab el-Mandeb Strait remains an economic lifeline for millions of people living in Ethiopia, Kenya, Somaliland, Somalia and elsewhere who rely on commercial goods imported from the Middle East and Asia. However, the Houthi forces in charge of increasing swaths of southwestern Yemen now control most critical ports and islands in the strait, increasing the risks and costs of transit and trade.

The strait has either been closed or has become a bottleneck, allowing only limited shipping traffic since September 2026. Many cargo ships have been delayed or rerouted, causing businesses in fragile regional economies to pass higher transport and fuel costs on to their customers.

The economic effects of costly and delayed shipping and trade through the strait has compounded the broader effects of increased violence and displacement throughout the region. In front of the U.N. General Assembly on Sept. 26, 2026, Djibouti foreign minister Abdoulkader Houssein Omar expressed “grave concern” about the sudden influx of Yemeni refugees putting a strain on underresourced coastal towns and refugee camps. The United Nations relief agency, UNHCR, is reporting an outbreak of cholera in the Markazi refugee camp, the primary home to thousands of Yemenis who have fled across the strait into northern Djibouti.

On top of that, the potential for a return to civil war in Ethiopia, and the potential involvement of Eritrea in regional conflicts, may increase population displacement and further disrupt economic markets on both sides of the strait.
As each of these conflicts unfolds, additional pressure will likely be put on the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. It provides the only feasible passage for many people seeking safety and opportunity abroad.

Keeping the Bab el-Mandeb open and safe is also vital for the delivery of humanitarian aid. Like challenges of commercial shipping, the maritime transit of relief supplies, including food and medicine, has been undermined by security risks, shipping delays and the rising costs of food and fuel.

UNICEF’s latest situation report for Somalia, published in August 2026, estimates that nearly 5 million people there are in urgent need of humanitarian assistance. At least another 5.5 million people in Ethiopia are also in need, due to the effects of conflict combined with below-average rainfall linked to El Niño.

In Yemen, an estimated 321,000 people have been displaced since Aug. 1, 2026, and ongoing water scarcity combined with conflict has left 17 million people without access to clean water, sanitation and hygiene services. As casualties mount and cholera spreads, hospitals have struggled to obtain essential supplies.

The Bab el-Mandeb Strait sits at the center of all of these crises. It remains a vital human and humanitarian corridor for millions of people needing refuge and relief. It is a lifeline as much as a geopolitical and economic linchpin.
Ensuring the safe passage of people and supplies of humanitarian relief through these waters is necessary to save lives and protect precarious livelihoods throughout the region.

articles.title: An atlas of vanished places: how climate change is rewriting the books on our shelves
articles.author: César Pablo Domínguez Prieto, Catedrático de Literatura Comparada, Universidade de Santiago de Compostela; University of Glasgow
paras: On August 26, 2026, a huge mass of rock and ice broke away at an altitude of around 5,200 metres in the Himalayas. Within minutes, it became an avalanche of debris and water that hurtled down towards the Nepal-Tibet border, with such force that the seismic signals were initially mistaken for an earthquake.

The region’s glaciers are visibly retreating, and thawing permafrost may well have contributed to destabilising these Himalayan slopes. Above all, the Nepal landslide illustrates something that will only become increasingly familiar: places that appear stable can change almost without warning.
While events like the Nepal landslide have an immediate, devastating impact on the people who live in these environments, they also leave their mark in a less obvious sphere: literature.

Biologist Rachel Carson’s 1951 book The Sea Around Us reminded readers that the boundary between land and sea has never been stable. Throughout our planet’s very long history, the oceans have advanced and receded. What makes the current situation exceptional is the speed of this transformation, as well as human activity’s decisive contribution to it.
Rising sea levels are one of its most visible manifestations. Since 1993, the global average sea level has risen by around ten centimetres.

And when a landscape changes, it also changes the world depicted in books. One scene from Lore Segal’s 2013 Half the Kingdom, for instance, takes place on a Brooklyn beach that a reader in the not-too-distant future might find submerged.

Philip Hoare’s The Sea Inside, also from 2013, explores coastal areas from England to Sri Lanka that may soon be underwater. The sandbanks of the Java Sea, where Joseph Conrad set his 1912 novel Freya of the Seven Isles, may have already been swallowed by rising sea levels.
When the landscape changes, these works all stay the same. Instead it is we, as readers, who change.
Leer más: Three things historical literature can teach us about the climate crisis

The field of comparative literature has long been exploring how works take on new meanings as they circulate across eras and cultures. Climate change adds an unexpected dimension to this problem: the future can also influence the history of a work.

In 1888, Theodor Storm published The Rider on the White Horse. The novella’s protagonist, Hauke Haien, studies geometry and applies his knowledge to the construction of new dykes on Germany’s North Sea coast, convinced that they will stand for centuries. A major flood tests both Haien’s engineering feat, and humanity’s confidence in our ability to master the sea.

Storm, of course, was writing before global warming, but today we – unlike the author and his original readers – know that the conditions that determine the behaviour of coastlines are changing. This allows us to read his story differently today. Not because we have discovered what Storm “really meant”, but because we are reading it from a different future.

Something even stranger can happen with the settings of literary works. Texts that we used to see as realistic might start to seem fantastical to us because they describe landscapes that no longer exist. And some works of fantasy might go the other way.

In Edgar Allen Poe’s only novel, 1838’s The Narrative of Arthur Gordon Pym of Nantucket, the author imagined a temperate region in Antarctica. When the book was published, it was a fantastical vision, but how will someone a hundred years from now interpret it?
Leer más: The Antarctic ice sheet is melting. And this is bad news for humanity
Part of our library could thus become, without changing a single word, an unwitting atlas of vanished places. This is what lies at the heart of my research on literature, oceans and climate change.

Books do not predict the future, nor can they replace climatology, glaciology or oceanography. They do something else: they preserve experiences of places, and connect timelines that no single human life can encompass. When the world changes, landscapes do not disappear from the page – they remain there, exactly as they were. What changes is the way we read them.

articles.title: Bond has always reflected the masculinity of his time – Robert Pattinson’s 007 will need to embody a new era
articles.author: Monica Germanà, Reader in Gothic and Contemporary Studies, University of Westminster
paras: James Bond has always reflected the cultural anxieties and zeitgeist of his era.

Sean Connery’s Bond embodied the confident western post-second-world-war masculinity of the early cold war. George Lazenby brought the character’s emotional vulnerability to light, reflecting the upheavals of the late 1960s. Roger Moore’s performance, meanwhile, added camp humour, theatricality and escapism in the 1970s.

In keeping with Ian Fleming’s more psychologically complex literary creation, Timothy Dalton brought a darker, more ruthless Bond to the screen. Stripping away much of the Moore era’s comedy and camp, his portrayal foregrounded emotional intensity and moral ambiguity. This reflected late-cold-war anxieties as geopolitical certainties unravelled and new threats emerged.

Next up, Pierce Brosnan incarnated a glamorous post-cold-war masculinity, with his lingering sexism teased out by Samantha Bond’s witty Moneypenny and the disruptive casting of Judi Dench as M, the head of MI6. And in the 2000s, Daniel Craig’s Bond was a physically tough but emotionally vulnerable character. His wounded body and scarred mind linked emotional detachment to childhood trauma.

Pattinson’s acting credentials make him one of the most established actors to take on the role. Since the Twilight saga (2008-2012), he has grown to be among the more versatile actors of his generation, with a penchant for challenging, often downright strange roles.

From the psychological intensity of Good Time (2017) to Robert Eggers’s claustrophobic gothic The Lighthouse (2018), the characters he has played are anything but straightforward leading men. Even when turning to action, his Batman (2022) was unexpectedly brooding and introspective.
There is certainly scope with his casting to extend the darker vision of Bond first introduced by Dalton and subsequently developed by Craig.

Visually, too, Pattinson seems almost a composite of previous Bonds. Declared the world’s most handsome man in 2020, Pattinson has the chiselled good looks of Brosnan. Although he might not have Connery’s physique, the intense training he underwent for Batman suggests that he could manage the demanding physical aspects of the role. This, however, may be more challenging, given that Pattinson, at 40, is already ten years older than former producer Barbara Broccoli had anticipated the next Bond would be in 2024.

As a white Englishman whose image is associated with an upper-middle-class, heterosexual masculinity, Pattinson might seem a safe, even predictable, choice for Bond. And yet, he is not unfamiliar with the challenge of portraying unconventional masculinity.

In Little Ashes (2008), he explored the young Salvador Dalí’s intimate relationship with the poet Federico García Lorca. Much like Craig, he has shown himself willing to explore queer desire and the instability of masculine identity.
I think what Craig’s era could have done more with is humour, and Pattinson might well bring a fresh comic sensibility to the next incarnation of Bond.

Beneath his often brooding intensity lies a nuanced comic performer. Humour has allowed Pattinson to question conventional masculinity in some of his roles. In Damsel (2018), he challenged the traditional western hero by playing an inept cowboy whose masculine confidence far exceeded his capabilities. Elsewhere, his darkly camp rendition of Louis the Dauphin in The King (2019), the tragi-comic The Drama (2026) and the self-aware short Fear & Shame (2017) all seemingly serve to undermine male vanity.

Perhaps Pattinson’s history of darkly strange and funny characters will create space for this new Bond to, playfully or otherwise, explore our current preoccupations with toxic masculinity, sexual consent and male vulnerability.

Fleming thought of his secret agent as an “unobtrusive … neutral figure – an anonymous blunt instrument”. Screenwriter Steven Knight now faces the challenge of using Bond as a blank canvas to highlight the clash between the character’s traditional roots and modern culture.
In particular, the new Bond would benefit from a more diverse supporting cast whose backgrounds are woven naturally into the story, reflecting his global audience without feeling forced.

I’m thinking female characters not defined by their relationships with Bond, villains who call out Bond’s elitism, queer characters that could complicate his seemingly straight world. Bond girls and villains will play a crucial role in delivering these (or failing to do so). But it will be Pattinson and his choices for this iconic character at the centre of it all, deciding whether the franchise will sink or swim.

articles.title: Making injustice legal: How Israeli law legitimizes apartheid, genocide and impunity
articles.author: Walid El Houri
paras: Israel’s laws are built to entrench ethnic domination, and international courts are under attack for noticing
Originally published on Global Voices
Roadblocks at the entrance to Shuhada Street in Hebron, Palestine. Photo by Travel 2 Palestine on Flickr (CC BY 2.0).

This post is part of Global Voices’ November 2026 Spotlight series, “Justice as infrastructure.” In this Spotlight, Global Voices is partnering with The Hague Institute for Innovation of Law (HiiL) to highlight the ways justice functions as critical infrastructure for any society. You can support this coverage by donating here.

Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank are subject to Israeli civil law. Palestinians who suffer their violence and occupation are subject to Israeli military law. The two face two different legal systems.

Palestinian, Israeli and international rights groups, and UN findings, have long argued this is not a malfunction of Israeli justice but its design, and that the international system meant to check, and failed to do so, is being taken apart.
Two legal systems, one occupation
For years, Israeli military data has shown conviction rates for Palestinians in Israeli military courts to be anything between 99.74 and 96 percent.

A May 2025 report by Adalah, the legal center for Palestinian citizens of Israel, documents how Israel moved settlement governance in Area C under civilian authority while Palestinians remain under military rule. Adalah calls the arrangement a system of apartheid and de facto annexation.

Inside Israel, the Knesset keeps adding to the structure. Adalah’s Discriminatory Laws Database listed over 65 laws that discriminate against Palestinian citizens of Israel or residents of the occupied territory in 2017. Its November 2025 report reviews more than 30 further laws passed between October 7, 2023 and July 27, 2025, which Adalah says rest on the principle of Jewish ethno-national supremacy that the 2018 Nation-State Law enshrined.

In March 2026, the Knesset passed a death penalty law with 62 votes. Adalah and four other Israeli rights groups argue its wording excludes Israeli Jewish perpetrators of similar offenses, so that in practice it applies only to Palestinians. They have petitioned the Supreme Court to annul it.

The Israeli group Yesh Din has tracked police investigations into settler violence against Palestinians since 2005. Of the files it monitored through 2025, 93.6 percent ended without an indictment, and only about 3 percent ended in a full or partial conviction. Most closures cited an unidentified suspect or insufficient evidence, which Yesh Din attributes to police failures. In roughly half of the nearly 30 mass settler attacks it documented between 2023 and late 2025, soldiers or police were present.

Soldiers face similar odds. In March 2026, the military’s top lawyer dropped charges against five reservists accused of severe sexual and physical abuse against a Palestinian detainee at the Sde Teiman detention camp. Yesh Din said only two indictments existed over soldiers’ conduct in the Gaza war.
Courts have not interrupted the pattern. In March 2025, Israel’s Supreme Court unanimously rejected a petition by five Israeli rights groups seeking unimpeded humanitarian aid into Gaza.
The UN Commission of Inquiry concluded in September 2025 that Israel committed genocide in Gaza, joining findings by Amnesty International and B’Tselem.

In October 2026, the commission added that Israel committed crimes against humanity in the West Bank, including extermination, and that military operations since January 2025 caused the largest displacement there since 1967.
Sanctioning the world courts

In July 2024, the International Court of Justice ruled that Israel’s presence in the occupied territory is unlawful and must end as rapidly as possible. It also found that Israel’s legislation and measures breach Article 3 of the International Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Racial Discrimination (ICERD), which prohibits racial segregation and apartheid. In September 2025, UN experts criticized the failure to act on the General Assembly resolution that followed the ruling.

Meanwhile, the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former defense minister Yoav Gallant in November 2024. In December 2025, its Appeals Chamber rejected an Israeli challenge and left the warrants in force.

The reaction to the warrants, like that to the UN findings regarding apartheid, genocide and crimes against humanity perpetrated by Israel, has contributed to the failure of international law in delivering justice.

By August 2026, nine of the court’s 18 judges and both deputy prosecutors were sanctioned by the US. On October 9, 2026, the US sanctioned the ICC itself, citing its jurisdiction over US nationals abroad, after earlier sanctions on three Palestinian human rights groups and UN special rapporteur Francesca Albanese. Human Rights Watch and three other groups have sued in US federal court, and say the aim of the sanctions is to shield US and Israeli officials from prosecution.

None of this is an aberration of the post-October 7 period, a rogue government or a failure to apply the rules. Adalah traces these laws to Israel’s constitutional and political culture, built on Jewish ethno-national supremacy, and notes that, unlike apartheid South Africa or Jim Crow in the US, “most of the laws cited in the report use neutral legal language.”

The UN Commission of Inquiry reaches the same conclusion from another direction. It traces the root causes back to 1947–1948 and says the aim of seizing maximum land while minimizing the Palestinian population stems from Israel’s colonizing policies.

That is how settler colonial states have always worked. Law does not sit outside the project. It is the project’s instrument. Military rule in the West Bank rests on emergency regulations the British Mandate wrote in 1945 to subdue the local population. Declaring “State land” has been, in Adalah’s words, the primary legal mechanism for taking Palestinian land since the late 1970s. Each layer converts dispossession into a legal procedure: a permit denied, a file closed, a petition dismissed, a statute passed.

Seen this way, the evidence describes one logic working across three levels. Statutes define who holds rights. Police, prosecutors and courts decide whom those rights protect. And the Israeli state has moved to shield itself from outside scrutiny, backed by a US government that now sanctions the institutions that try to apply international law.
A state built to secure one people’s dominance over another people’s land will produce exactly this legal order.

articles.title: Civil society questions decree that could block access to telecommunications networks in Mozambique
articles.author: Masudul Zarif
paras: Officials claim the measure ‘protects society,’ but civil society organizations see a threat to freedom of expression
Originally published on Global Voices
Post-election protests in Maputo, Mozambique, in 2025. Photo by Wilson Thole. Used with permission.

Civil society organizations in Mozambique, such as the Center for Democracy and Human Rights (CDD), submitted a document to the Ombudsman contesting the constitutionality of Decree No. 48/2025, issued in December 2025, which establishes control mechanisms and potential blocks on access to telecommunications networks in the country.

According to the portal Moz24h, journalists and experts are concerned that the measure could threaten rights such as freedom of expression, access to information, and communication, particularly in contexts of social mobilization or political tension. The challenge arises in an environment still heated from the conflicts following the 2024 elections.

Activists and civil society actors argue that the decree could enable restrictions on access to the internet and digital platforms — tools that have become increasingly central to the circulation of information, the organization of protests, and civic participation. The approved text allows the state to suspend telecommunications services for up to 48 hours without needing a court order, reports Deutsche Welle.

Also, according to civil society organizations, the decree grants broad powers to authorities to intervene in telecommunications networks on grounds of national security or the maintenance of public order.

By appealing to the Ombudsman, the organizations are requesting an analysis of whether the decree is compatible with the Constitution of the Republic of Mozambique, as well as Mozambique’s international commitments regarding human rights and freedom of expression.

In March 2026, the Minister of Communications and Digital Transformation, Américo Muchanga, denied that the measure restricted rights. He defended it as a way to protect society in critical moments, strengthening the state’s capacity to manage crises and protect critical telecommunications infrastructure.
Experts diverge in their reading
In discussions with Global Voices, various experts presented different interpretations of its potential impacts.

One researcher, who asked not to be identified for security reasons, recalls that several democracies around the world have legal mechanisms allowing temporary restrictions on communications. For the researcher, political contexts where social demonstrations are frequently interpreted as threats to stability can make the application of this type of legislation particularly sensitive. He notes:

O que foi feito neste decreto é tentativa de legalizar toda e qualquer ação que o governo possa ter em uma situação de protesto social. Na França existe, no Brasil existe, nos Estados Unidos existem. Em qualquer parte em que exista alguma democracia, que chamamos a dita democracia consolidada, existem dispositivos estatais, governamentais, que limitam o acesso às comunicações, quando se entende que eles violam o direito de outras pessoas ou imposições em causa do próprio Estado. Não é o decreto o problema. O problema é como pode ser aplicado. O nosso problema é que não há tolerância. Tudo aquilo que parece ser protesto é visto como tentativa de subversão, tentativa de colocar em causa a ordem. É um problema histórico de governança e questão central na interpretação também do próprio decreto.

What was done in this decree is an attempt to legalize any and all actions the government might take in a situation of social protest. It exists in France, it exists in Brazil, and it exists in the United States. Anywhere there is some form of democracy, what we call so-called consolidated democracies, there are state, governmental mechanisms that limit access to communications when it is understood that they violate the rights of other people or impose demands against the state itself. The decree is not the problem. The problem is how it can be applied. Our problem is that there is no tolerance. Everything that looks like a protest is seen as an attempt at subversion, an attempt to jeopardize order. It is a historical problem of governance and a central issue in the interpretation of the decree itself.

Meanwhile, activist and journalist Nadio Taimo emphasizes that the decree comes at a time when Mozambique’s digital civic spaces face growing pressure. According to him, internet access has become fundamental for the circulation of information and the exercise of freedom of expression. Taimo observes that many media outlets migrated to digital platforms because of the high costs of traditional printing, making the online environment an important space for news dissemination, public debate, and social mobilization. In this context, potential blocks on internet access could significantly limit access to information.

Já temos uma expansão, uma onda crescente de jornais eletrônicos. Já não imprimimos jornais, devido aos custos. Migramos para a era digital, logo, há aqui um bloqueio de acesso à informação, e até o próprio espaço de opinião, de promoção da liberdade de expressão, pode ser limitado. Os órgãos de comunicação social são todos, a maior parte deles, do governo, e controlados, e nos é fechado o espaço cívico, o espaço físico, nas ruas, quando nos proíbem de realizar marchas.

We already have an expansion: a growing wave of electronic newspapers. We no longer print newspapers due to costs. We migrated to the digital era; therefore, there is a block on access to information here, and even the very space for opinion, for promoting freedom of expression, can be limited. The media outlets are all — most of them — government-owned and controlled, and our civic space, the physical space in the streets, is closed to us when they prohibit us from holding marches.
The activist further adds that the decree could formalize practices that, according to civil society organizations, have already occurred during moments of political tension:
Este documento é apenas uma formalização de uma intenção política de bloqueio da internet, que já vinha sendo aplicada, só que não havia uma formalização legal.
This document is merely a formalization of a political intention to block the internet, which was already being applied, only without a legal framework.
Precedent cases: Protests and control

The debate over telecommunications control in Mozambique is also linked to previous episodes of social mobilization. In February 2008 and September 2010, mass protests in the cities of Maputo and Matola were triggered by the rising cost of living, particularly the prices of transport and essential goods. During those demonstrations, mobile phones and text messages were widely used to mobilize and coordinate actions. In response, the government at the time promoted stricter communications regulation measures, including mandatory SIM card registration for all users.

New protests broke out again in November 2012 as young people protested the fare hikes for urban semi-collective transport, locally known as chapa-100. Swift intervention by police forces in areas with the highest concentration of protesters prevented the demonstrations from spreading.

These episodes occurred during defining moments of social demand by Mozambican youth in the post-independence period (1975), reflecting frustrations over economic inequalities, unemployment, and the rising cost of living amid economic liberalization. In this scenario, urban culture also played an important role in expressing social discontent. Artists like the rapper Azagaia became influential voices among young people, with social critique songs widely broadcast during demonstrations and across digital platforms.
A regional trend of internet shutdowns

The debate in Mozambique is not an isolated situation. International digital monitoring organizations have documented numerous cases of internet shutdowns in African countries in recent years, often linked to electoral processes, popular protests, or internal conflicts. In Angola and Guinea-Bissau, for instance, blocking or restricting internet access has been utilized by governments during periods of political instability.

Human rights organizations and digital freedom advocacy groups argue that shutdowns limit access to information, hinder the work of journalists, and restrict civic participation, while digital governance experts warn that such measures can have significant impacts not only on public debate, but also on the livelihoods of the civilian population.

Despite the ratification of the aforementioned decree in Mozambique, its practical application has not yet been documented, making it difficult to assess its potential effects in practice. Concurrently, the Constitutional Council has not yet ruled on civil society organizations’ position regarding the decree’s potential unconstitutionality, contributing to a landscape of legal and institutional uncertainty.

articles.title: Eurovision Asia: a diverse and spectacular showcase of Asian pop
articles.author: Jess Carniel, Associate Professor in Humanities, University of Southern Queensland
paras: On November 14, Asia fired up its wind machines and pyrotechnics for the inaugural Eurovision Song Contest Asia, aka Eurovision Asia.

Eleven countries competed – from Bangladesh and Bhutan to Vietnam and host country Thailand. Notably absent this first year were most of the continent’s most populous nations: China, India, Japan, Pakistan and Indonesia.
The format was familiar: three-minute songs performed with no more than six people permitted on stage. But there was a distinct regional inflection in the staging, costuming and language choices.
Many of the artists wove in elements of traditional sound and traditional dress, and artists expressed gratitude to the audience with the traditional Thai gesture wai (hands together).

While the original Eurovision is hosted in a combination of English and French, Eurovision Asia was delivered in English only. But most artists performed either in their own language (36%) or a combination of that language with English (54%). Only South Korea’s song was performed entirely in English.
By comparison, Eurovision 2026 featured 43% of songs entirely in English, 38% in languages other than English, and 19% multilingual.

Musically, it was a diverse offering. The delicate lotus leaves of Vietnam’s Tóc Tiên and her back-up dancers broke into a high-energy opening number, Em Tiên. Malaysia’s Aina Abdul finished the show with a pitch-perfect power ballad, Bluest Sky.
In between, audiences were treated to Cambodian and Bhutanese ballads, Bengali a capella, South Korean K-pop and, perhaps most surprisingly, Nepali rock.

But it was the Philippines’ Carmelle – the youngest contestant, at 19 – who won the night with Sobra-Sobra. The focus of the empowering pop song in English and Tagalog was about Filipino women’s right to be who they want to be.
“It’s about how unapologetic, independent and strong Filipinas are. It describes me – not just me, but of course all the Filipinas,” Carmelle told The Guardian.
Carmelle received 211 points, winning both the jury and the public vote, encompassing viewers from 183 countries and territories.
With her victory, the Philippines has won the right to host Eurovision Asia in 2027. In the meantime, Carmelle will also perform at the 2027 Eurovision Song Contest in Bulgaria.
Eurovision is known for its spectacle, and Eurovision Asia delivered, albeit on a more modest budget. Stage production made the most of stunning visual projections, smoke and flares.
Eurovision is also known for its non-political stance, with political or ideological messages prohibited.

But it has been more forgiving toward humanitarian statements. And at Eurovision Asia, Nepal’s Pratik Himal Rai used the end of his set to call for support for his country as it recovers from the August flood disaster.

The show was not without its hitches. Laos’ representative, Thinla, couldn’t hear her music due to an issue with her earpiece, so footage of her technical rehearsal was shown at the end of the performances to ensure fair judgement of her act.
Thai artists Mang x Daou experienced wardrobe malfunctions during their ballad Aroma, though this didn’t affect their chances in the voting – Thailand came in second place, with 169 points.
If Europe has Eurovision, why can’t Asia have Asiavision?
For one, the name “Asiavision” is already taken: it’s the broadcasting network of the Asia-Pacific Broadcasting Union (ABU), which has its own song contests and festivals.

But mostly, it’s about branding. Although the name Eurovision has become synonymous with the song contest, it actually refers to the European Broadcasting Union’s (EBU) pan-European telecommunications network.
The Eurovision Song Contest was created in 1956 to promote the network and attract audiences across borders. (No, it was not created to unite a war-torn Europe.)

The purpose of Eurovision Asia is specifically to expand the Eurovision brand and format into the region. This is a project the EBU has been attempting for more than two decades. It plans to continue the expansion of the brand through other continental editions.
The future of Eurovision Asia
Staging the inaugural competition is one thing, but securing the longevity of the franchise in Asia is another matter.

Buy-in from economic powerhouses Japan, China and India may be the key to its success. Negotiations were underway with China and Japan to participate this year, and organisers are optimistic that they and several others will join in 2027.
The broad geographical scope of “Asia” also has the potential to draw in participants from the Middle East.
But broader participation presents its own challenges.
The original Eurovision is heavily associated with LGBTQIA+ acceptance and pride, which may not be well-received by certain broadcasters and their audiences within Asia.
We saw this play out in the inaugural Eurovision Asia contest: Malaysian broadcaster TV3 cut drag performer Vice Ganda, the Phillipines’ jury spokesperson, from its broadcast.
There was also speculation about whether Islamophobia played a role in Malaysia’s Aina Abdul’s results; despite being a favourite to win going into the contest, she finished in fourth place.
Like the OG Eurovision, Eurovision Asia offers great potential for soft power politics.

It also has the potential to be a powerful global platform for Asian pop. The inaugural competition was a diverse showcase for the unique voices and cultures of its participants, beyond the dominant trends of J- and K-pop. Hopefully we will get a chance to see more in Manila next year.

articles.title: Madagascar aims to support biodiversity by protecting marine areas
articles.author: Rebecca Cluett
paras: In Madagascar, biodiversity goals are being tested by funding challenges and local realities
Originally published on Global Voices
A booth at COP17 showcases Madagascar’s local communities and biodiversity. Photo by Sary nalain'ny mpanoratra. Used with permission.

At the 17th Conference of the Parties (COP17) on biological diversity, held October 19–30, 2026, in Yerevan, Armenia, Madagascar reaffirmed its commitment to protecting its remarkable biodiversity and showcased techniques local community members have implemented.

The country further outlined its plans and priorities for the future and promoted the initiatives it is committed to in order to protect both its terrestrial and marine ecosystems. This conference was also a strategic opportunity to strengthen green partnerships, develop new collaborations, and to engage with national and international stakeholders involved in biodiversity conservation.

To mark the occasion, Global Voices interviewed Tojotsara Ratefason, Director of the Directorate of Protected Areas, Renewable Natural Resources, and Ecosystems (DAPRNRE), part of the Madagascan government’s Ministry of Environment and Sustainable Development (MEDD), at this conference. The interview focused on Madagascar’s role in implementing the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, the 30×30 global target, conservation funding, and the vital role of local communities, women, and young people in the sustainable protection of Madagascar’s natural heritage.
Watch the full interview in French here:
Raveloaritiana Mamisoa (RM): Where does Madagascar stand on implementing the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework?

Tojotsara Ratefason (TF): Madagascar est confiante dans sa capacité à contribuer à l’atteinte de l’objectif mondial 30×30, aussi bien pour les écosystèmes terrestres que marins. Notre pays dispose déjà d’un système d’aires protégées qui constitue un socle essentiel pour préserver sa biodiversité exceptionnelle. Selon les chiffres que nous présentons, ce réseau compte 155 aires protégées terrestres et marines. Il s’agit d’un acquis important sur lequel nous pouvons nous appuyer pour poursuivre nos efforts de conservation. Madagascar dispose d’un cadre national de référence pour orienter ses actions en faveur de la biodiversité : la Stratégie et le Plan d’Actions Nationaux pour la Biodiversité (SPANB). Ce document définit les grandes orientations du pays en matière de conservation, d’utilisation durable et de valorisation de son patrimoine naturel exceptionnel. Il s’inscrit dans le cadre de la Convention sur la diversité biologique, à laquelle Madagascar est partie, et constitue un instrument essentiel pour traduire les engagements internationaux en actions nationales. Mais la protection de la biodiversité ne se résume pas au nombre d’aires protégées ni aux superficies concernées. Notre objectif est avant tout de préserver les écosystèmes, les espèces et les habitats naturels qui font la singularité de Madagascar. Notre patrimoine naturel est unique au monde et nous avons la responsabilité de le transmettre aux générations futures. Cette ambition implique également de renforcer la collaboration avec les communautés locales (vahoaka eny ifotony), qui vivent au contact direct de ces ressources naturelles. Leur participation est indispensable, car la conservation ne peut pas reposer uniquement sur les décisions du gouvernement. Elle doit être portée conjointement par les institutions publiques, les gestionnaires des aires protégées et les populations qui vivent dans les territoires concernés. Nous devons donc trouver les moyens de travailler ensemble, dans une démarche de responsabilité partagée. Les communautés locales doivent comprendre l’importance de la biodiversité, participer à sa protection et pouvoir constater les bénéfices qu’elles peuvent tirer de sa conservation. C’est également dans cette perspective que le Ministère de l’Environnement et du Développement Durable cherche à promouvoir les emplois verts et les opportunités économiques liés à la biodiversité unique de Madagascar. Notre richesse naturelle ne doit pas seulement être considérée comme un patrimoine à protéger : elle peut aussi représenter une source de revenus et de développement pour les populations, à condition d’être valorisée de manière durable. L’enjeu est de permettre aux communautés de mieux connaître la valeur de leurs ressources naturelles, d’en être fières et de comprendre qu’elles ont tout intérêt à les préserver. Lorsque les populations constatent que la conservation contribue à améliorer leurs conditions de vie, elles peuvent devenir des partenaires encore plus engagés dans la protection de leur environnement.

Tojotsara Ratefason (TF): Madagascar is confident in its ability to contribute to achieving the global 30×30 target, for both terrestrial and marine ecosystems. Our country already has a system of protected areas which forms the foundation for preserving its exceptional biodiversity. According the figures we are presenting, this network includes 155 terrestrial and marine protected areas. This is a significant achievement on which we can build to continue our conservation efforts. Madagascar uses a national reference framework to guide its actions to support biodiversity — the National strategy and Action Plan for Biodiversity (SPANB). This document defines the country’s general direction in terms of conservation, sustainable use, and enhancing its remarkable natural heritage. It is part of the Convention on Biological Diversity, of which Madagascar is a signatory, and is an essential for translating international commitments into national actions. However, the conservation of biodiversity is not limited to the number of protected areas, nor is that the sole area of concern. Above all our aim is to preserve the ecosystems, species, and natural habitats which are distinct to Madagascar. Our heritage is unique in the world and we have a responsibility to pass it on to future generations. This ambition also requires collaboration with the local communities who live directly alongside these natural resources. Their involvement is indispensable as conservation cannot rest solely on the decisions of the government. Decisions must be jointly taken by state institutions, those who manage the protected areas and the populace of the regions concerned. Therefore, we must find ways to work together and to share the burden. It is important that local communities understand the importance of biodiversity and participate in its protection and can see the benefits that they can raw from its conservation. It is in this vein that the Ministry of the Environment and Sustainable Development is looking for ways to promote ‘green’ jobs and opportunities linked to Madagascar’s biodiversity. Our natural wealth should not only be seen as a heritage to be protected: It can also present a source of revenue and development for the population, as long as it is used in a sustainable way. The challenge is allowing communities to better understand the value of their natural resources, to be proud of them and that it is in their interest to preserve them. Once populations realize that conservation can help improve their living conditions, they can become even more committed partners to protecting their environment.
RM: What finance is available for conservation and how is it used? And how does the government ensure that these resources actually benefit local communities?

TR: Madagascar dispose d’un atout majeur pour mobiliser des financements en faveur de la biodiversité : notre pays figure parmi les 17 pays mégadivers au monde, reconnus pour la richesse exceptionnelle de leur patrimoine naturel et l’importance de leurs espèces endémiques. Cette reconnaissance renforce l’importance de Madagascar dans les efforts internationaux de conservation de la biodiversité. Notre pays a également bénéficié de financements du Fonds pour l’environnement mondial (FEM), connu sous son sigle anglais GEF (Global Environment Facility), qui soutient des projets environnementaux. Toutefois, au-delà de la mobilisation des ressources financières, notre objectif est de faire en sorte que ces financements puissent atteindre les communautés locales. Les populations vivant à proximité des aires protégées jouent un rôle essentiel dans la préservation des écosystèmes et doivent pouvoir bénéficier concrètement des efforts de conservation. Nous devons donc veiller à ce que les financements consacrés à la biodiversité ne servent pas uniquement à soutenir les activités de protection de la nature, mais contribuent également au développement des communautés concernées. Il est important que les populations locales puissent tirer des bénéfices de la conservation, notamment à travers des initiatives économiques durables et des activités génératrices de revenus compatibles avec la préservation des ressources naturelles. L’enjeu est de concilier la protection de notre patrimoine naturel avec l’amélioration des conditions de vie des populations. La conservation doit être une responsabilité partagée, mais aussi une opportunité pour les communautés locales. En constatant les bénéfices concrets de ces actions, elles pourront s’impliquer davantage dans la protection de la biodiversité malgache.

TR: Madagascar has a major advantage when it comes to securing funding for biodiversity. Our country is one of the world’s 17 megadiverse countries, recognized for the exceptional richness of their natural heritage and the importance of their endemic species. This recognition reinforces the importance of Madagascar in international efforts in biodiversity conservation. Our country also benefits from funding from the Global Environment Facility (GEF), which supports environmental projects. At the same time, as well as mobilising financial resources our aim is to ensure that these funds reach local communities. Communities living near the protected areas play an essential role in preserving ecosystems and should receive concrete benefits for the conservation efforts. We must, therefore, ensure that the funds allocated to biodiversity are not only used for nature conservation but that they also contribute to the development of local communities. It is important that these local communities can see the benefits of conservation particularly through sustainable economic initiatives and income-generating activities that are compatible with the preservation of natural resources. The challenge is to reconcile protecting out natural heritage with the improvement in living conditions of these local communities. Conservation should be a shared responsibilty but also an opportunity for local people. By seeing the concrete benefits of these initiatives they will get more involved in protecting Madagascan biodiversity.

articles.title: Mass protests that led to regime change had their heyday between 1980 and 2011: what happened?
articles.author: Ida Rudolfsen, Senior researcher, Peace Research Institute Oslo (PRIO)
paras: People are taking to the streets across the world. In 2025, mass mobilisation occurred in countries such as Morocco, Tanzania and Turkey. In Madagascar, protests resulted in president Andry Rajoelina fleeing the country in October. More recently, protesters have filled the streets from France and Italy to Senegal and Kenya.
By mass mobilisation, we mean sustained, organised campaigns of protests that involve more than 1,000 people, aimed at changing a country’s political regime or removing the government or leader.

Mass mobilisation has historically been seen as a viable path to democracy. Ferdinand Marcos left Manila in 1986 after weeks of popular protests. The Berlin Wall fell in 1989 after months of demonstrations in East Germany. South Africa’s apartheid regime yielded to domestic and international pressure in the 1990s.
The examples are many, and mass movements have been a driving force to democratic change in authoritarian regimes.

Yet the historical record is less clear-cut. We are researchers who study protest and democratisation. In a recent study, together with colleagues Kristian Skrede Gleditsch (University of Essex) and Gudmund Hermansen (University of Oslo), we examine how mass mobilisation influenced the likelihood of democratic transitions between 1900 and 2019.

We find that the well-documented relationship between mass mobilisation and democratisation largely belongs to a historical golden age, stretching from the early 1980s until roughly the Arab Spring in 2011. During this period, mass mobilisation was strongly associated with both democratisation and regime change.

Before and after this golden age, however, we find no detectable relationship between mass mobilisation and democratic change. The two periods are nevertheless not identical. Before 1980, mass mobilisation made rulers more likely to fall. But the regimes that fell were not systematically replaced by democracies. In other words, mobilisation could topple a regime, but not necessarily bring about democratic change. One example is Ethiopia’s 1974 revolution. Mass protests and strikes contributed to the overthrow of Haile Selassie, only for the monarchy to be replaced by a military dictatorship rather than democracy.

Today, the pattern is different. From the Arab Spring through 2019, mass mobilisation is no longer systematically associated with regime collapse. Authoritarian regimes have managed to remain in power despite extensive mobilisation. Major waves of protest have challenged incumbent regimes without bringing them down. Authoritarian leaders increasingly appear capable of riding out even large-scale popular mobilisation. Examples include Belarus, Iran and Togo,

At the same time, we are witnessing exceptionally high levels of popular mobilisation. The fact that it no longer has the same democratising effect helps explain how a wave of protest can coincide with the current authoritarian wave.
Understanding why mass mobilisation on democratisation has become less effective is one of the most important questions for understanding the development of democracy in our time.
Why has mass mobilisation become less effective?
The short answer is that we do not know for certain.

To examine how the effectiveness of mass mobilisation has changed over time, we combined data on protest campaigns demanding democratic change to classify countries as democracies or autocracies in each year. We focused only on autocracies, examining whether mass mobilisation increased the likelihood of a transition to democracy. Unlike previous studies, we used statistical models that allowed the effect of mass mobilisation to vary over time, rather than assuming it remained constant.

We also tested whether our findings depended on a few influential cases. More than 20 campaigns that were followed by democratic transitions during the golden age would have had to end without democratisation to substantially flatten the peak. Similarly, around 10 unsuccessful campaigns after 2010 would have needed to result in democratic transitions to substantially reduce the observed decline.
The overall pattern also held when we excluded individual regions from the analysis.

We find little support for several suggested explanations. Trends in campaign size, the diversity of participants, coordinated leadership, state repression, and where protests take place do not coincide with the rise and fall in protest effectiveness.

However, our measures are relatively crude, so we cannot rule out that these factors played a role. But they are unlikely to explain the broader pattern on their own. What we can show is that the power of mass mobilisation to bring about democratic change has shifted dramatically over time. What we cannot say with certainty is why its golden age began, or why it came to an end.

Some scholars have suggested that today’s movements may have become overly dependent on social media and large demonstrations, whereas effective resistance requires deeper organisation, a wider range of tactics, and long-term relationship-building. Our data do not capture these factors well enough to provide a decisive test of that argument.

At the same time, authoritarian regimes may have become better at responding to challenges from the street. New information technologies make it easier to monitor opposition movements and identify key individuals. This facilitates what researchers call smart repression: more targeted and subtle forms of coercion.

The international climate may also have contributed to this shift. The golden age coincided with the end of the cold war and stronger international pressure for democratic reform. But since the Arab Spring, western countries have increasingly chosen stability and security cooperation over democratic reform.

At the same time, authoritarian regimes have gained access to alternative sources of support. Contemporary autocracies operate through international networks that provide one another with money, technology, propaganda and diplomatic backing. They may strengthen regimes’ capacity to withstand mass mobilisation.

Our study doesn’t conclusively test these explanations. Together, however, they suggest that the rise and fall in the effectiveness of mass mobilisation is unlikely to be explained by any single factor.
Perhaps the pendulum has begun to swing back?
Nor can we say with certainty what effect mass mobilisation has on democratisation today.

Our analysis ends in 2019. We do not know whether the weak relationship we observe at the end of the period has persisted, or whether the pendulum has started to swing back. Historically, the impact of mass mobilisation has moved in cycles. It was by no means obvious in the 1970s that the world was on the verge of a golden age of democratic mobilisation.

Since 2019, moreover, we have seen several important victories for mass mobilisation. In Bangladesh, Sheikh Hasina was forced from power following extensive student protests. In Serbia, nearly two years of student-led protests culminated in an electoral victory that ended Aleksandar Vučić’s long hold on power. In South Korea, popular mobilisation helped stop President Yoon Suk Yeol’s attempt to sideline democracy. And in Poland and Hungary, broad democratic mobilisation has formed part of a wider resistance to governments that ultimately lost power through elections.

In Senegal, mass protests in 2024 helped thwart President Macky Sall’s attempt to remain in power beyond his constitutional mandate. In Malawi, mass protests against electoral irregularities, alongside judicial intervention, paved the way for an opposition victory in the 2020 rerun election.
Democratic courage is therefore clearly not in short supply.

Researchers may try to understand what is required, but it is above all those who continue to organise, demonstrate and demand democratic rights and freedom for everyone who can ensure that it happens.

articles.title: Learning under trees in the era of AI: The paradox of education in Mozambique
articles.author: Masudul Zarif
paras: AI could help bridge educational inequality in a country where thousands of students still learn outdoors
Originally published on Global Voices
Photo taken by Rahul Ingle, May 2012. This file is licensed under the Creative Commons Attribution 2.0 Generic license.

In many communities across Mozambique, formal education still takes place in the open air, under trees, in improvised yards, or inside fragile structures that barely offer protection from the sun and rain. These so-called outdoor classrooms are not an innovative pedagogical choice, but more often than not, the expression of a structural deficiency: a lack of infrastructure, a shortage of materials, and an estimated deficit of around 12,000 teachers in 2025.

During the rainy season (roughly November to March in Mozambique), the situation becomes more challenging. In several regions, the school calendar must be adjusted to respond to inclement weather, such as heavy rains that disrupt classes and hinder the continuity of teaching between November and March each year.
In this context, the question arises: What is the place of artificial intelligence (AI) in an educational system that, in many areas of the country, is still fighting for the basics?

In rural districts of provinces like Cabo Delgado, Nampula, and Zambézia, it is common to find classes of students studying under trees. The Minister of Education, Samaria Tovela, has been evaluating schedule adjustments because, while classes are frequently interrupted during the rainy season, concentration becomes a constant challenge during periods of intense heat. Without proper blackboards or textbooks, and often with a single teacher responsible for several classes, the learning process becomes irregular and deeply unequal when one million students learn to read and write on the ground.

This scenario highlights a central problem: Learning depends on minimum standards that are not yet guaranteed in Mozambique. At the same time, one of the biggest obstacles to introducing technologies like AI in rural African contexts is the lack of connectivity. In Mozambique, about 73 percent of the population lacks internet access, according to 2024 data from the Ministry of Transport and Communications.

Regional inequalities limit these initiatives, despite some progress recorded in recent years. This limitation directly affects the potential of solutions such as distance learning or digital learning platforms.
Language, culture, and the role of the state

Another critical challenge is the linguistic and cultural dimension. In Africa, where more than 2,000 languages are spoken, only a fraction — around 49 — are represented on digital platforms like Google’s translation service. Integrating Mozambique’s Indigenous languages, such as Emakhuwa, Xichangana, or Elomwe, into digital educational tools could significantly increase students’ comprehension and engagement, especially in the early years of schooling. However, implementing these solutions raises practical questions in contexts where access to technology is still limited.

The overwhelming majority of the Mozambican population speaks a Bantu language most frequently at home (81.7 percent), and a portion cannot speak Portuguese at all (41.9 percent), though it is the sole official language of the country due to its colonial history. Despite this, the media, official government communications, and healthcare institutions continue to privilege Portuguese to the detriment of Bantu languages — the languages of the masses — which, activists argue, constitutes a form of social exclusion. Emerging initiatives, however, show that it is possible to bridge this gap with the aid of technology. In Johannesburg, for instance, tech startups are developing AI solutions tailored to African languages.

Offline tools, pre-loaded content, and digital pedagogical assistants are some of the possible solutions to address the deficiencies and limitations of Mozambique’s education system. While the government does not yet have specific policies to integrate AI tools in schools, advocates say the state could play a central role in integrating technology into the daily lives of students and teachers. This also involves investing in teacher training; ensuring basic infrastructure; facilitating energy access; and strengthening partnerships with universities, startups, and international organizations.

Talking about artificial intelligence in outdoor classrooms may seem contradictory at first glance, but it is precisely in these contexts that technology needs to be considered creatively and responsibly, not as a replacement for the essential, but as a strategic complement.

The priority remains clear: Building schools, training teachers, and ensuring access to basic materials. The question is how to integrate developed technology without creating profound inequalities, respecting local contexts, and placing the student and teacher at the center of decision-making. In a country where learning still takes place under trees, the future of education will depend not only on the technology available, but also on the political and social choices that define who has access to knowledge and under what conditions.

articles.title: Letter from a jailed Azerbaijani political prisoner reveals deadly consequences of silence
articles.author: Global Voices Eurasia
paras: The Trump administration’s blind eye to severe human rights violations in Azerbaijan is deadly for political prisoners
Originally published on Global Voices
Bahruz Samadov being brought to Sabail District Court in 2024. Image by Voice of America, via Wikimedia Commons. Public domain.

This post is part of Global Voices’ November 2026 Spotlight series, “Justice as infrastructure.” In this Spotlight, Global Voices is partnering with The Hague Institute for Innovation of Law (HiiL) to highlight the ways justice functions as critical infrastructure for any society. You can support this coverage by donating here.

Bahruz Samadov is an Azerbaijani political scientist, peace activist, and PhD candidate at Charles University in Prague, or at least he was until the summer of 2024. On August 21, 2024, the State Security Service detained Samadov while he was visiting his grandmother in Baku. Global Voices reported on his arrest at the time, as part of a wider crackdown on critics before Azerbaijan hosted COP29 in November 2024.

Samadov was one of the few Azerbaijani voices to oppose the 2020 Karabakh war. In his writing for OC Media, Eurasianet and other outlets, he argued for dialogue with Armenia and criticized the expulsion of ethnic Armenians from Karabakh. Prosecutors charged him with high treason based on his WhatsApp exchanges with Armenian peace activists and on publicly available information. Samadov denied the charges and called himself a “prisoner of peace.” His lawyer argued that the prosecution’s theory of “indirect espionage” was vague and had no basis in case law.

On June 23, 2025, after a closed-door trial, the Baku Grave Crimes Court sentenced him to 15 years in prison. The Baku Court of Appeal upheld the verdict in September 2025, and the Supreme Court did the same in September 2026. Amnesty International, which considers him arbitrarily imprisoned, reports that he has been held in solitary confinement and denied medical care, and that he has twice attempted suicide, most recently in his Supreme Court hearing. Below, Global Voices publishes a letter Samadov wrote from prison and asked us to share.

The 2024 summer holidays ended in a nightmare: while visiting Baku, my home city, from my doctoral studies in Prague, I was detained by the notorious State Security Service of Azerbaijan and soon was charged with “high treason.” Studying the ideological tenets of the hegemonic regime in my homeland, I directly connected its durability to the conflict between Azerbaijan and Armenia, revealing the narratives of “national unity” under the “savior strongman.” During and after the outbreak of the 2020 War in Karabakh, I criticized the deployment of military means. Between 2021–2024, I partook in various conferences and meetings across Europe, presenting my perspective and calling for a meaningful and inclusive policy of peace and co-existence. The Azerbaijani regime, having years of the crackdown experience, is aggressively intolerant to any kinds of contestation, and especially targets the independent academic voices. When the repressive machinery was re-launched in late 2023, the regime started the total crackdown on civil society, independent media, politicians, and academicians. In private communications, more than five political prisoners connected it to the worsened relations with the Biden administration. The latter was highly critical to the human rights violations in Azerbaijan. Weeks before leaving the White House, Blinken invited human rights defender Rufat Safarov to Washington to receive the Human Rights Defender Award. Several hours after visiting the US Embassy in Baku, Safarov was arrested and accused of hooliganism and fraud. It was an open signal to the US that the leaving administration had no power to endorse the Azerbaijani critical voices. The Azerbaijani government acted differently with the Trump administration. The August 8, 2025 meeting and the peace agreement was the soon-disappeared sign of hope for us. Even if the peace agreement did not include any references to human rights, the current administration’s plans for the long-term involvement in the region brought hopes for at least minimal reforms in Azerbaijan. Curiously, my sham trial was “fastened” and ended on June 23, 2025 — a process too explicitly controversial to the “peace agenda.” Following the US delegation’s visit to Baku in January 2026, a number of political prisoners, me among them, appealed to the US officials to raise the “political prisoners issue” to the official Baku — a policy that once partially worked during Obama’s second term. However, the recent severe sentences and USA’s silence prove our call remained rather a mere cry from the chamber cells. The Baku-based team of Toplum TV, the veteran human rights defender Anar Mammadli and others have received up to 15 years of imprisonment. To compare, the EU Parliament recently adopted a resolution calling for the release of political prisoners in Azerbaijan. Similar calls were made by the PACE and even the UN. Meanwhile, the Trump administration is proud to end the violence in the South Caucasus (by the way, this narrative is implicitly contested by the official Baku — there D. Trump remains a mere “witness.”) While the Administration of White House endorses officials like Hikmet Hajiyev for their nice compliments to D. Trump and villanization of “Biden–Blinken couple,” the sufferings of Azerbaijani imprisoned dissent keep going. Many of those fellow political prisoners I had a chance to talk to remain pessimistic and sceptical regarding the US involvement in the region, dismissing the possibility of the “Belarusian scenario.” One prominent political prisoner even rejected to sign the aforementioned call: “They came for security-related issues, they do not care about human rights,” he shouted from the cell’s balcony. “We are Biden’s prisoners,” laughed my inmate, an imprisoned journalist and poet. True, nothing publicly known has been made by the Trump administration related to severe human rights violations in Azerbaijan. If the Republican administration aspires to replace Russia in the long-term in the South Caucasus, it should not abandon the ideals of the Founding Fathers in the foreign policy standards. Washington has officially repeatedly mentioned the human rights violations in rival countries like Iran, Cuba, and formerly Venezuela. The selective attitude to the human rights issues and turning the blind eye to our suffering endangers the democratic security of the US itself, not to mention its international image. This policy raises questions about the adherence to the American ideals of the current administration. Yet, it is still not too late to follow the recommendations of Amnesty International: “Use every available opportunity, in bilateral and multilateral forces, to raise concerns about Azerbaijan’s human rights record.” Bahruz Samadov Umbaku Prison 27.10.2026

Samadov’s arrest and his continued imprisonment are clear examples of the breakdown in justice mechanisms within Azerbaijan. While the current U.S. administration and other international observers continue to remain silent on this breakdown, others are calling on the government to stop weaponizing the court system and are looking for mechanisms to reform this vital infrastructure.

articles.title: A new Democratic Congress will view Trump’s harsh Cuba policy skeptically – but that doesn’t mean a change is coming soon
articles.author: Joseph J. Gonzalez, Associate Professor of Global Studies, Appalachian State University
paras: The so-called “blue tsunami” that hit the United States in the midterm elections is causing ripples around the world.
Having won a historic victory, congressional Democrats now appear poised to challenge the Trump administration’s conduct of foreign affairs.
The Iran war, support for Ukraine and the management of Venezuelan oil certainly all appear to be on the agenda of some Democrats.
The flipping of the House and Senate from Republican to Democratic control has also led to speculation that members of Congress may also wish to challenge Trump’s Cuba policy.

After all, the United States’ position on Cuba has swung in recent decades, depending on the balance of power in Washington. An easing of tensions and normalization of relations between the U.S. and Cuba took place under the presidency of Barack Obama, only to be reversed following the election of Donald Trump in 2016. President Joe Biden largely followed Trump’s lead, while making more allowance for activities supporting the Cuban people.

In his second term, however, Trump has pursued an even harder line than before. Since January 2026, the administration has instituted a devastating economic and fuel blockade, prohibiting Cubans from importing oil. This pressure tactic is meant to get the Cuban government to agree to increased economic privatization and political democratization.
While the Cuban government has met certain demands, notably with respect to the economy, it has resolutely refused to change either its personnel or its authoritarian character.
The result of this blockade has been a stalemate and increased hardship for Cubans. As a historian of U.S.-Cuban relations, I saw that hardship firsthand during a visit to Havana in June 2026.

While I understand the notion that emboldened Democrats may try to force a change in direction of the Trump administration’s foreign policy, including on Cuba, I doubt they will be able to do so. In fact, there are reasons to believe that the midterm results may actually reinforce Republicans’ hard-line approach to the Caribbean island.
Since 1961, at the height of the Cold War, the U.S. government has enforced a rigorous sanctions regime against communist Cuba – the longest-running embargo in modern history.

In January 2026, the Trump administration made that embargo even more severe with the oil importation ban, part of a regional pressure campaign that also saw U.S. forces abduct and remove from office Venezuela’s President Nicolás Maduro, a longtime ally of the Cuban government.
For Cubans, no oil means no electricity. Blackouts, already a problem, have become longer and more frequent.

Absent electricity, Cubans have no regular access to running water. Disease, from mosquitoes, other pests and unsafe water, has increased dramatically. Cuba’s once much-praised medical system often cannot treat patients unless they bring their own drugs and supplies.
Inflation has soared and tourists have stopped coming, while industrial and agricultural production has declined dramatically.

Cubans hate the U.S. embargo for contributing to this misery. At the same time, many also blame their government. During my last visit, Cubans I spoke with told me that they believe their leaders are more concerned with protecting their power and privileges than with the welfare of the average Cuban.
For many Cubans, this indifference explains why President Miguel Díaz-Canel and his allies have rejected the Trump administration’s central demand of surrendering their monopoly on power.
Trump’s demands, blockade and the threat of military force have led to some concessions by Cuba’s leaders.
During the past year, Cuba’s government has released some political prisoners and permitted greater foreign investment, most notably from Cuban Americans.
The government in Havana has also expanded the range of legally permitted private enterprise in Cuba.

But when it comes to the question of power, Díaz-Canel and his allies remain implacable. They know that relinquishing power will cut off the supply of profits from state-owned businesses that flows their way and maintains their opulent lifestyles.
They also argue that Trump has no right to determine the rulers of a sovereign nation.
Rubio’s ideological priority
For the moment, it appears that Díaz-Canel hopes international and domestic politics will compel Trump to turn his attention from Cuba.
No doubt, the “blue wave” of the U.S. midterms has encouraged that belief. If so, I believe the hopes of the Cuban government are probably misplaced.
This is in large part because U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, a Cuban American who formerly represented Florida in the U.S. Senate, remains determined to topple the Cuban government.

Rubio has long been a foreign policy hawk and fervent proponent of regime change in Cuba. As secretary of state, he has also been a key figure in the Trump administration’s push to expand American power across Latin America and support right-wing movements and governments.
It is also no secret that Rubio wishes to succeed Trump as president. That has not changed since the midterm elections.

In order to become the Republican nominee for president, Rubio will most likely need to win Florida’s primary. And if he is to win the White House, Rubio will surely need Florida’s electoral votes, especially in light of the results of last week’s election in Texas, which saw a U.S. Senate seat and the governorship turn Democrat.

Rubio’s path to the presidency will be easier if he continues to enjoy the support of South Florida’s Cuban American community, which favors regime change by an overwhelming margin and represent a powerful voting bloc in Florida.
In short, I believe ambition and ideology will provide Rubio with the impetus to refuse all compromise with what remains of Cuba’s communist government.
Interestingly, some Republicans seem uneasy with aspects of America’s Cuba policy, particularly the emphasis on investment opportunities as opposed to democratic change.

Nonetheless, Trump has reasons to push harder on Cuba. The midterm results show that his domestic agenda – and the war in Iran – are vote losers. He may see toppling the Cuban government as a guaranteed “win” for him and his administration, both in terms of legacy and in the eyes of voters.
Of course, Democrats in the new Congress could deny the administration funds to maintain the oil blockade or, in an extreme case, invade Cuba.
Democrats could also exercise Congress’ powers of investigation and oversight.
Though these measures enjoy some support among Democrats, it is far from certain that House or Senate leaders would support them.

After all, the Democratic Congress has other priorities that appear of greater concern to the American people, such as the Iran war, not to mention domestic policy issues, such as healthcare and an “affordability agenda.”

Moreover, Democratic leaders may regard efforts to end the oil embargo as politically risky: Such efforts could alienate voters in Florida and divide the Democratic caucus, some of whose members favor the embargo.
Outside of Florida, Americans generally disapprove of U.S. policy toward Cuba. But they are unlikely to demand that their representatives force the administration to change course.

With the pressure on Democrats over Cuba relatively low, and their priorities elsewhere, the Trump administration will likely face little opposition to maintaining the embargo until it can say that it has achieved its political and strategic objectives.
Meanwhile, members of Cuba’s governing elite, without appealing alternatives, will likely look to cling to power as long as they can.
And the Cuban people will continue to pay the price.
